We have found that this assumption necessitates specific relationships among entropies calculated using monogamy of mutual information, and these relationships can be satisfied by solutions to Einstein's equations where the matter energy-momentum tensor is directly proportional to the Ricci curvature. Notably, this theory includes solutions where the boundary entropy is constant.

This research investigates two dependent lattice models, the $U_{n}$ and $M_{n}$ models, which we analyze together as a combined model, the $QM_{n}$ model. We examine the modular group actions on the bases of the model's state space, applying the branching rule to compute local state probabilities. We then verify specific conjectures proposed by Gu and Zhang based on our calculations. We also derive explicit expressions for the weights of the $QM_{n}$ model, establish a connection to pre-Weyl algebra via a quantum separation of variables, and finally prove exact correlation functions for the dependent $U_{n}$ and $M_{n}$ models.

This research investigates how the integration of various stabilization methods, including projection, regularization, and constrained optimization, affects a group of signal recovery algorithms. We reveal that even though these techniques are applied at different stages, their effect can be profound. Our findings suggest that recovery methods work best when all data are accurately reconstructed before any stabilization is employed. In cases where some data must be approximated, we discovered a method to choose an optimal stabilization procedure. This approach not only enhances algorithm performance but also provides profound theoretical insights into the properties of the problem, including dual certification for certain methods. To validate our findings, we developed a set of experiments and real-world applications, such as MRI image reconstruction, where we successfully used generalized gradient methods in conjunction with optimized stabilization, achieving superior results compared to established methods.

Nonlinear coaddition algorithms like median and clipped-mean are effective at removing outliers in astronomical images, but they can't ensure a consistent point spread function (PSF) for stellar objects. We've developed a new nonlinear coaddition method, the weighted clipped-mean algorithm, based on a robust statistical concept. This approach maintains a stable and constant PSF for objects, while simultaneously eliminating data outliers and removing background variations. We tested the accuracy of our method by comparing synthetic and real-image evaluations with another established technique.

We establish that the chordal SLE driven by a BESQ process is equivalent to growing an imaginary surface in a complex $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ space in such a way that its real projection maps to a tree structure. This imaginary surface can be visualized as a collection of growing primary follicles that branch into secondary ones, with their growth rates determined by a secondary BESQ process. These findings provide a unique mathematical framework for understanding the SLE tree structure and its scaling properties, offering a direct visualization of the SLE process in the $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ space and its relationship to quantum conformal field theories.

This study aims to present and discuss a novel, non-iterative proof for the Navier-Stokes equations' well-posedness in a maximum norm. This proof follows the same structure as that initially proposed in [L.T. Beding, 2016], but has been modified to accommodate certain changes. By building on this framework, we can derive a corresponding transport equation's well-posedness in a maximum norm. Our transport equation analysis has implications for the Navier-Stokes equations as well as other similar systems, effectively providing an alternative proof for those equations' well-posedness in a maximum norm.

This paper proposes an improved protocol for verifying quantum circuits, CVQC. It enhances the previous qstate verification protocol to support verification of complex circuits that incorporate unitary and unitary-related elements. CVQC leverages circuit agnostic proof systems to verify the correct behavior of circuits, but the protocol comes with a significant cost: its verification process is significantly slower than other verification methods. In 2021, a revised protocol was published, but the key issue remains unresolved. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing an optimized protocol that significantly speeds up verification. Compared to the previous protocol, CVQC is now nearly 50% faster while maintaining the same verification accuracy. Additionally, CVQC is now more efficient, with which it is possible to verify complex circuits that were previously out of reach. Notably, the improved protocol is significantly faster than other verification methods, such as classical compilation or circuit simplification. CVQC is now the most complex verification protocol, with which it is possible to verify circuits of over 150 qubits. Finally, the authors suggest future directions for fully homomorphic verification of quantum circuits.

The remarkable ability of deep generative models to create synthetic data that mirrors real-world patterns is opening up a wide range of possibilities in image processing and learning within biology. In this study, we leverage this potential to enhance cell tracking and segmentation tasks by generating cell shapes from time-lapse microscopy data. By employing a generative adversarial network to learn the statistical properties of intact, dividing cells, we create an extensive library of synthetic cells. This dataset allows us to develop a robust prediction model, which can predict missing information in video sequences experiencing partial loss due to limitations in imaging technology. In comparison to existing methods, our approach outperforms them significantly on actual cell division data. Furthermore, this framework has the added benefit of facilitating the analysis of hypothetical cell trajectories that would be difficult to obtain experimentally. Therefore, this study demonstrates the practical utility of deep generative models in improving image recognition tasks while also enabling novel scientific explorations.

Recent research in the field of reinforcement learning has demonstrated that feature persistence significantly impacts performance in geometric tasks. This study investigates how using composite features, which can persist, affects the sample efficiency in reinforcement learning tasks. The investigation reveals that using persistent features decreases sample efficiency, which motivates the examination of a supervised learning problem to understand the underlying cause. The analysis shows that high-dimensional composite features contain unnecessary information that causes overfitting, leading to a suboptimal model. The removal of this unnecessary information can be achieved by applying a technique called information matrix squared test. This paper provides a computational approach for performing in-depth feature analysis and promoting causal representation learning, which can also be applied to reinforcement learning environments that utilize a sparse reward design to encourage causal feature representations.

To capture the complex behavior of magnetic suspensions, we developed a three-dimensional model of ecologically friendly magnetic dipoles. The model simulates Newtonian dynamics by incorporating Brownian movements and dipole-dipole interactions. It lacks the freeze-out issue seen in some higher-dimensional dipolar models. To further simulate real-world scenarios, we added spherical obstacles of varying size and introduced a depletion attraction between them at a certain temperature below the critical value. The model exhibits diverse collective behaviors, such as glassy states, tetrahedral structures, and clustering depending on the size of the primary units, depletion attraction strength, and volume of the obstacles.

Data augmentation significantly enhances sound event detection (SED) performance, but its optimal application remains unclear. This study identifies and addresses two critical issues related to data augmentation in SED: (1) the lack of a standardized process for creating training datasets, and (2) the absence of a method to control the magnitude of temporal transformations. To resolve these problems, we introduce a multi-stage end-to-end model that incorporates data augmentation, and a new error type called $L_1$-error. Based on experimental results with DCASE 2019 task 3, our proposed approach yields superior performance compared to the baseline model that utilizes the standard $L_2$-error. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of various data augmentation methods and propose a set of rules to ensure the creation of high-quality training datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that increasing the magnitude of temporal transformations can lead to overfitting in SED systems.

The principle of superposition in communication and computing technologies is fundamental, with its implications extensive and complex. This paper conceives the superposition property as a universal concept, encompassing various domains from physics and engineering to mathematics and logic. By examining the superposition property through the lens of truth tables and Boolean functions, the authors reveal the existence of irreducible sets that facilitate novel mathematical structures, as well as the potential for safeguarding private data in federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access systems.

This research introduces a novel spectrogram feature extraction method rooted in signal detection and estimation theory. Our approach leverages level sets to identify relevant data patterns within the spectrogram, and associates each level set with a corresponding signal orientation. Each signal orientation is characterized by an intrinsic mode, which serves as a marker for that particular level set in the spectrogram. Our method effectively captures one-dimensional data patterns cross-sectional to the time-frequency axis, and is illustrated through its application to noise removal in a sample signal.

We utilize the difference of spectra technique to identify the number of synchronized clusters in a group of coupled chaotic systems, each comprising multiple individually synchronized groups. Our method enables the determination of the number of synchronized clusters even in cases where direct observation is challenging. Furthermore, we outline a procedure for extracting the corresponding eigenvalues associated with each clustered group. Our approach is demonstrated using two sets of coupled rings with varying parameters: the Elzeegat and the Wang system.

We introduce a new verification module within the OpenMDA framework, enabling the creation of reliable models that accurately predict the behavior of complex physical systems involved in molecule interactions. The module facilitates the development of appropriate input data required for solving nonlinear partial differential equations through the solution of corresponding ordinary differential equations. Verification of the new module involves testing its capabilities against established benchmarks, specifically the Squeezed Michelson interferometer, the Nitrogen Molecule, and the Hydrogen Atomic Clock, all representing distinct categories of molecule interactions.

In recent years, researchers have proposed using quantum systems as "engines" that convert randomness into work. A key component of these systems is a switch that allows them to operate in an "on" state, producing output work when needed. A common approach to measuring this switch involves clicking a Geiger counter, turning the switch off after measurement. This limitation can be overcome by using continuous measurement, allowing the switch to remain active. However, the process of implementing continuous measurement in quantum systems is intricate and influenced by various factors. In this study, the authors provide a comprehensive explanation of continuous measurement and demonstrate its effectiveness in a quantum system without a pointer, a setting in which efficiency is maximized when the switch and its opposite state are equally probable.

In a study on the mechanics of dense disk packs, researchers discovered that 
jamming occurs over a broad range of weights for individual disks, with their 
jamming characteristics largely dictated by the disk's shape and the confining 
space, rather than their weight. Using a novel, ultra-sensitive torsional force 
sensor, researchers were able to accurately measure the jamming torque - a 
direct indicator of the gel-like rigidity found in these dense disk packs. 
Jamming torque was found to be highly dependent on the disk's shape and the 
confining space, while its jamming temperature remained relatively unaffected. 
This research lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the mechanics of 
complex, dense particle packs and their applications in temperature-controlled 
systems.

Research indicates that various forms of El Ni$\~{a}$o and La Ni$\~{a}$a exhibit distinct precipitation patterns in South America. To better understand these differences, a statistical model was created to generate high-resolution precipitation datasets for South America, using only atmospheric pressure data. This model was then used to produce a set of 15 years of simulated data, matching the period of the observed anomalies. By comparing the simulated results to real precipitation data, the accuracy of the model was confirmed. Furthermore, the capability of the model to capture the unique characteristics of each event type was validated. By applying the inverse of the model to the entire 15-year period of average-sized anomalies, a new high-resolution dataset was produced, covering the entire continent. This reversed dataset can help represent uncertainty in regions where there may not be sufficient data.

The initial black hole seeds can be categorized into two types: heavy seeds, formed through the collapse of massive gas clouds, and light seeds, created by the infall of smaller gas clumps. A parameterized model has been developed to study heavy seed formation, incorporating various physical processes, and comparing its results to observations, specifically the ultraluminous pulsar heart radio source HE1357-6028. This model excels at reproducing the black hole's observed spectral energy distribution, but cannot account for its radio emission. On the other hand, a different model is needed to explain the source's radio emission. However, both models fail to perfectly explain the entire spectrum of this exceptional object.

Recent breakthroughs have made dense topological matters accessible through artificial materials and single-crystal production. Research on these systems has shown that flat bands, which exist within specific lattice structures, significantly impact correlation effects. Studies have primarily focused on single-band systems, although flat bands can also be found in multi-band systems. We have discovered that flat bands can induce strong correlations in three-band systems that feature non-trivial connections between orbitals. We have applied numerical methods to study the properties of an octahedron lattice model that exhibits two distinct flat bands. One band is created by combining orbital correlations, while the other is a result of inter-site interactions. These two bands do not intersect, allowing us to establish a mapping to an effective single-band model. We have analyzed the phase diagrams of this model, observing the emergence of various correlation-driven states, including a Mott insulator, heavy Fermion, and $U(1)$ spin liquid. Our findings demonstrate that flat bands in multi-band systems can give rise to unique correlation effects that can be explored in artificially designed topological matters, single-crystal systems, and other flat band hosts.

By examining the relationship between protein sequences and SNPs associated with phenotypes, researchers gain insights into the interior workings of the genome. Previous studies using bioinformatics to identify internal genome mechanisms focused on the expression of genes. This study uses data from the 100K SNP dataset and the UniProt protein database to analyze the relationship between protein sequences and SNPs associated with complex diseases and traits. Results show that sequence variations affecting protein function are more relevant to certain diseases and traits, while variations affecting protein structure are more important for others. The impact of disease and trait-associated SNPs that lie outside of protein-coding regions can be considered marginal. The risk-related effects of SNPs within genes are mostly explained by variations occurring within protein-coding regions, indicating that these variations interact with each other to influence risk.

In this study, we are investigating the existence of 2-designs featuring a prime power number of points that also possess a group of automorphisms consisting of a semi-simple non-abelian group. We have established that such a 2-design with a prime power number of points cannot exist if its size is less than 34152 points. Moreover, we have discovered that the only 2-designs fulfilling these conditions are those isomorphic to $H(64, 15)$ and $H(12169, 346)$.

Within the Hohenberg-Kohn density functional theory, the generalized Coulomb correlation effect is investigated in confined electronic systems confined at the $n$sphere potential. The focus is on the informational entropies of one-body and two-body reduced density matrices, and how they are affected by the correlation. The findings show that the entropy associated with the Coulomb correlation is a measure of it, and it relates to the classic entropy in bulk systems. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the entropy associated with the Coulomb correlation in bounded systems can be approximated using the thermodynamic limit, and it increases as the bounding potential decreases. The study also reveals that the Coulomb correlation has a significant impact on the entropies of bounded systems confined at the $n$sphere potential, and the entropy associated with the Coulomb correlation in such systems depends on the number of electrons, the sphere radius, and the sphere charge. The findings of this study can be useful for understanding the general properties of bounded systems, and how the generalized Coulomb correlation effect affects their electronic structure and the associated entropies.

The precise measurement of wide binary star systems' velocity dispersion is crucial to understanding their age and formation history. Accurate measurement relies on high-reliability individual star velocity measurements, especially for small systems. Our team developed a line velocity measurement method using a least-squares algorithm and incorporated star color information to improve its precision. We applied this method to data from the Gaia EDR3 and WDS catalogs for 13 wide binary star systems, obtaining more precise individual star velocity measurements than previously possible. Our results reveal a significant improvement in measurement accuracy when using two color information, rather than just one. Furthermore, incorporating star parallax measurements also enhances precision. We compared our results with existing data and found the star velocity measurements we obtained align well with expectations, indicating the usefulness of our line velocity method for analyzing additional wide binary star systems in the future.

Cut-elimination in multiplicative linear logic results in the partial elimination of structural rules when combined with a strategy, yet this process does not necessarily guarantee the erasure of all structural rules when considering multiple inputs/outputs and cut-elimination becomes less predictable. A previously introduced method focuses solely on the strategy's ideal representation, potentially leading to confusion between the strategy's computational content and ideal form. A more recent introduction compromised on predictability to distinguish between the two. A reliable separation between the computational content of a strategy and its ideal representation has yet to be established. A group of semantics seeks to separate the two by focusing solely on the semantics' interpretation, typically resulting in an ambiguous middle ground between the computational content and ideal form. A semantics is introduced which focuses neither on the strategy's computational content nor its ideal representation, instead focuses on an otherwise unrelated aspect, then uses a syntax to separate the strategy's computational content and ideal form through a decoupling syntax. A similar decoupling syntax is introduced in the proof structure to separate the logical content and algebraic content. A cut-elimination procedure is introduced which only removes cuts whose algebraic content matches the proof structure's algebraic content. As a result, the partial order of the domains of variables is preserved during the proof structure's cut-elimination, and the logical content remains intact.

Previous studies have explored the application of machine learning and non-linear dynamics to analyze and forecast the synchronization between time series, particularly focusing on predicting the synchronization state for specific time points. This study introduces a novel deep learning approach that not only identifies synchronization states but also estimates the corresponding time interval until the time series become synchronized. This model was evaluated and validated using time series data from the S&P 500 and Euro Stoxx 50 indices, with the results showing that deep learning can be a viable alternative to other methods for the synchronization task.

To effectively manipulate chemical reactions, controlling the vibrational states in the reactants is crucial, especially since we can influence non-adiabatic transitions using these states. However, coupling these modes with quantum states is challenging, which is why we explore the idea of utilizing bound-bound transitions and extend it to apply to vibrational modes. Our method relies on optically driving a specific vibrational mode in one of the fragments to induce an electronic transition and transfer control of the vibrational state, potentially across reaction pathways. Using a study on the collision of water with a flat surface, we demonstrate how to selectively activate modes that contribute to the degradation of a surface-bound water molecule. Our proposed technique offers a new approach to controlling chemical reactions at the quantum level.

Predicting the click-through rate (CTR) is a vital aspect of online advertising, and to enhance accuracy, many studies incorporate visual elements, such as images and logos, into their models. Research has demonstrated the significance of visual features in CTR prediction, and data from ad platforms like Google DoubleClick CLS (Connected Learning Sandbox) supports further exploration of this area. In this study, we investigate the contribution of visual elements, specifically visual IDs, on a large scale of advertisers and learnings from real-world experiments can guide industry professionals in effectively utilizing visual information to boost CTR predictions. Our analysis reveals that combining visual information with textual data leads to improved CTR prediction performance, and by analyzing the relative importance of visual elements, we can adjust our models to place greater emphasis on these elements, ultimately enhancing overall results. To achieve this, we use the SHAP (SHapley Value-based ADminiated Pair) method for visual ID importance evaluation. Additionally, our experiment on a real-world scale in Google DoubleClick CLS shows that using visual information leads to increased profits by up to 8.42%. In conclusion, our findings underscore the value of incorporating visual information in CTR prediction models and provide CTR researchers with practical insights on how to utilize visual data in their studies. To support future research, we have released our code and data for public access.

The concept of fairness in concurrent system execution has garnered attention within the realm of Business Process Management (BPM). Current approaches primarily rely on testing techniques to detect potential system deadlocks. However, these methods fall short in providing a comprehensive understanding of the system's behavior, particularly failed transitions and the resultant processes. To address this limitation, we propose an original algebraic technique for designing a dissociative operator that ensures a given process can be completed by activating a specified number of activities. The proposed operator is part of a composite operator for the construction of multi-threaded processes, where the order of execution of guard statements is non-deterministic. Based on this operator, we develop an algorithm for multi-process dissociative generation. Subsequently, we introduce the associated operation in the flow expression language and its underlying algebra, along with the fundamental properties of this operation. Finally, we present an iterative algorithm for dissociative generation of multi-processes, which enables the simultaneous generation of processes with a specified number of active threads.

This study employs a statistical method influenced by physics to model the interaction of light with airborne particles by leveraging Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). Our approach uses real-world data to establish relationships between environmental factors and aerosol optical depth (AOD) levels, thereby enhancing model generalizability and applicability to specific scenarios. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, we compare predictions from the standard SFIS Monte-Carlo simulations with our statistical model, utilizing multiple observational datasets to inform our analysis.

This research introduces a novel Bayesian statistics framework to preserve privacy in location-based services when dealing with data that has a specific spatial pattern and was collected in a sequential manner. It addresses the issue of lost privacy due to data relationships by leveraging a spatial process with built-in uncertainty to protect individual locations. Furthermore, we propose an efficient simulation method to calculate probabilities in large-scale scenarios, allowing for the incorporation of geostatistical techniques. To test the framework's effectiveness, we conducted several experiments, including real-world data analysis from the Taxicab dataset, focusing on various metrics such as average proximity, entropy, and mean squared error. The framework outperformed a baseline method, yielding comparable results in terms of proximity and better results in terms of error. The framework achieved this through the use of a scale parameter that controls privacy loss and spatial correlation.

We conducted the first inter-site study investigating the reliability of functional connectivity changes using a node-magnitude approach. This study combined data from two large datasets collected from distinct sites: one dataset consisted of resting-state data from 1,052 individuals, including healthy controls and individuals with schizophrenia, and the other dataset contained resting-state data from 853 individuals, including healthy controls and individuals with depression. Our analysis revealed that the reliability of node-magnitude changes varied significantly across brain regions, with some regions showing high reliability coherently across datasets and others exhibiting low reliability. Notably, we observed that the reliability of inter-site site-interactions affected the detection of group differences, and that a combined analysis of within- and cross-site interactions enhanced the detection of group differences while reducing false positives. Overall, our findings suggest that a multi-dataset approach can significantly contribute to enhanced statistical power in brain research.

Building on the spirit of the heat interwoven with entropy, we initiative a heat-equation-based framework for concentration of measure inequalities. This framework will encompass the heat-interaction with measure, a concentration of measure phenomenon. We anticipate this framework to serve as a useful analytical tool, facilitating direct solution of integral curvatures issues, like diameter estimates and volume growth bounds, at an optimal level. We substantiate this idea by deriving fundamental concentration of measure inequalities for doubling-doubling metric-measure spaces, thereby providing novel, sharp, and simple diameter estimates, thereby generalizing known diameter estimates for these spaces, albeit our results are likely less precise than what can be obtained via other methods.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have led to significant improvements in code-mixed language modeling, but they still face a persistent challenge: a substantial performance gap between code-mixed and monolingual language models. Most existing approaches have concentrated on enhancing the modeling of multilingual sentences, while disregarding positional characteristics. Our study introduces a novel positional encoding technique for code-mixed language modeling, which effectively leverages position-specific characteristics and flexible sentence structures, such as multiple language switches. We have developed a multilingual positional encoding model that automatically detects language shifts in code-mixed text. We conducted thorough experiments with publicly available datasets for code-mixed English-Hindi and English-Tamil, which revealed that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art models by narrowing the performance gap with monolingual language models for sentiment classification and sequence labeling tasks. Notably, it achieved comparable performance with multilingual models on cross-lingual sentiment classification tasks.

Despite significant research efforts, the microscopic mechanisms driving superconductivity in hydrogen-sulfur systems remain unclear, especially since the isotope effect coefficient in these materials is highly uncertain. We employed ab initio calculations to investigate how varying nuclear masses affect the energy spectrum and dynamical responses in H$_3$S under various pressures, reaching high pressures similar to those found in Earth's upper mantle. We found that the unusual pressure-dependent behavior of $^1S_0$ superconducting pairing in H$_3$S arises from two distinct contributions, stemming from electron-phonon interactions and dynamical effects, respectively. While the electron-phonon interaction contribution behaves unexpectedly under pressure, the dynamical effect contribution exhibits a more straightforward response. Additionally, we explored the isotopic coefficients in H$_3$Te and found notable differences between these systems and their behavior under pressure. Our studies highlight the importance of considering both electronic and structural aspects when analyzing the superconducting properties of hydrides.

Bulmer's average effect concept has been re-expressed by others as the second moment of the distribution of gene substitutions over generations. Although the term 'average effect' is sometimes used to describe the fourth moment, which is thought to be more relevant to phenotypic changes, the correct association is with the moment that represents the squared change in allele frequency. When considering the changes in genotype frequencies, the fourth moment accurately represents the changes in phenotypic value, aligning with the idea that larger changes involve the replacement of one allele by another.

This research focuses on the advanced control systems of bipedal robots that utilize sensory feedback from sensors, including vision, to refine their gait patterns. By integrating the ideas of reinforcement learning and closed-loop feedback control, our approach can adapt the bipedal robot's movement strategies to effectively tackle unpredictable obstacles and ensure stable progression. Using simulation tools to simulate real-world walking scenarios, we successfully demonstrated that our control system can develop policies that regularly pause and look ahead, all while maintaining balance, which would be challenging for traditional planning methods to achieve. Furthermore, our PDDRL-controlled robot can successfully navigate and respond to novel situations in the AirLab's humanoid robot, HyAD.

We propose a new method that leverages learned camera descriptors and features
to improve 3D camera relocalization performance, particularly in complex and
difficult scenarios. Our approach combines standard point feature tracking with
two novel techniques: packed bundle adjustment descriptor matching, and a
deterministic strategy for resolving ambiguous pose solutions. Through rigorous
evaluation, we demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art
techniques, achieving an average localization error rate of 0.56 meters on the
TUM-RGBD dataset, outperforming other methods by approximately 0.1 meters.

In the context of federated learning, a personalization technique can significantly enhance the performance of individual clients. Our research investigates the semi-supervised learning domain, where a personalization technique based on few-shot learning is explored. Notably, prior studies in this area have limitations, as their theory assumes an ideal scenario where client data can be perfectly encoded and transmitted to the server without errors. Contrasting this, our work proposes a more realistic approach, where a personalizable semi-supervised learning model is developed under the condition that the server can select one or more clients for training. Our key contributions involve establishing theoretical bounds on the communication cost required to achieve a desired level of performance, as well as the development of an optimal strategy to minimize energy consumption by the server while maximizing the model's accuracy.

The magnetic field within an accretion disk formed from accretion debris of a neutron star is extensively regulated through differential rotation. As the neutron star dissipates its own spin energy, the magnetic field grows strongest near its inner boundary. A recent model indicates that, following a neutron star disruption, the inner disk of the accretion disk undergoes significant shrinkage, driven by the reduced angular momentum transferred from the remaining neutron star. Consequently, the inner disk's radial velocity increases, leading to an accelerated reduction in its magnetic field strength. Simultaneously, the outer disk's increased expansion leads to increased entropy, prompting a heightened rate of synthetic microphysical viscosity, thereby increasing the disk's total torque. This enhanced disk behavior results in a more rapid minimization of the inner disk radius, leading to a more pronounced inner hole formation. In the inner disk region, the magnetic field becomes sufficiently weak, enabling enhanced black hole spin-up and gamma-ray emission. Additionally, the increased entropy in the outer disk causes the emission of a higher electron-positron flux, leading to a reduction in the inner disk radius radius scale of about an order of magnitude compared to traditional models, with potential implications for post-merger system observations.

We've established a more direct proof of a cohomology sequence related to isomorphic classes of line bundles on compact Riemann surfaces, and we've also made clear the role of the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class in this context.

This study presents novel, rigorous criteria ensuring the existence of a unique, unique quasi-stationary distribution in Markov processes, along with exponential convergence near equilibrium. We demonstrate the validity of these conditions for a range of diffusion processes, including stable processes in higher dimensions and relativistic stable processes. Additionally, by combining these results with existing approaches, we derive sharp asymptotics for the probability of finding these processes outside a specific exclusion zone.

Optimizing the concentration of chemical species in graphene is crucial for achieving various physical responses. We examined the optical forces generated between graphene and a target particle under two distinct chemical species environments, one with a single energy level and another with two energy levels. In the case of a single energy level, we modeled the system's equilibrium state and demonstrated how the chemical potential's gradient could position the particle. Conversely, for particles within a two-energy level environment, we developed a set of non-trivial steady-states. By adjusting the chemical species' concentrations, we showed that the particles could be forced into specific, target patterns. These scenarios offer promising avenues for optimizing nanoscale machine development.

To better understand the impact of Emergency Department (ED) lengths of stay, researchers used a natural experiment in a large, urban hospital. They discovered that extending treatment time by 30 minutes beyond three hours resulted in higher within-30-day revisit and readmission rates. A one-month revisit rate increased by 16.5-29.5% and readmissions rose by 14.5-25.9%. This study aligns with prior evidence suggesting that prolonged ED stays are linked to increased healthcare utilization. By leveraging a natural intervention, researchers could quantify the exact visit rate increase associated with prolonged stays, unlike prior studies using patient propensity scoring. Additionally, revisit and readmission rates predicted from the model matched observed outcomes, indicating strong accuracy. Higher visit rates for patients initially admitted to the hospital or by the same physician were found, as well as higher readmission rates among patients transferred to other hospitals.

This study explores how multiple agents approach decision-making in a shared environment where some tasks are more challenging than others. The tasks vary significantly in terms of required attention and reward magnitude. Importantly, an agent's choice of task depends on not only its own current state but also the states of fellow agents, particularly the most accomplished agent. A model is developed to analyze how high-performing agents influence less skilled agents through their selection of tasks, which involves uncovering the optimal task difficulty based on an agent's current state and the state of the top-performing agent. A key finding shows that when tasks have distinct levels of difficulty, a stable situation often emerges where more capable agents focus on harder tasks, while less capable agents focus on easier tasks. Consequently, a hierarchical structure forms in which higher-ranking agents excel at more complex tasks, while lower-ranking agents focus on simpler tasks. Ultimately, this study provides insight into how cooperation can arise through the control of shared resources, even with significant differences in ability levels.

Our investigation focuses on the influence of background effects, tied to local charge conservation, on the measurement of charge-dependent correlations in heavy ion collisions. Using digital holographic simulations of collisions, we examined how these background effects are encoded in the photon production and found that they can significantly impact measurements of charge-dependent correlations. Our study highlights the importance of accurately accounting for these background effects when interpreting experimentally measured correlations in the context of strange particle production.

This study introduces an innovative approach to predict crowdfunding outcomes
based on cultural similarity between a project and existing projects in the same
field. Unlike other studies that only consider numerical data, our method leverages
textual representations of project descriptions to calculate cultural congruence with
relevant artistic movements, leveraging techniques like topic modeling and
cross-entropy. We also analyze the effect of audience demographics on fundraising
amounts. Our analysis reveals that cultural similarity is a more reliable predictor of
success than project features or creator demographics. Notably, the dynamics of
online crowds are less influential in determining fundraising outcomes than the
project's or creator's attributes.

In order to improve network intrusion detection systems, several organizations utilize machine learning, specifically deep neural networks, by sharing their expertise, but face challenges overening information due to data disparities and competing interests. The present paper proposes a unified framework combining federated learning and graph neural networks to address these issues. A novel, unsupervised anomaly detection method utilizing unlabeled data is presented, allowing multiple organizations to collaborate while preserving their privacy. A key advantage of our approach is enables collaborative learning without requiring sharing actual data. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves comparable accuracy to supervised methods while identifying attacks with accuracy similar to that of PNNs, thereby showcasing its potential for real-world applications.

Advancements in autonomous robotic technology depend heavily on sophisticated algorithms. The complexity of robotic tasks often necessitates their execution over an extended period, during which various factors can emerge posing unanticipated effects on performance. We've developed an approach to optimize robotic tasks by predicting and adapting to such dynamics. We model the phenomenon of tasks evolving during execution using change detection theory and leverage this model to anticipate changes before they occur. Based on such predictions, we modify the original task or create a new one to ensure successful task completion. We test our approach in simulated Scenarios, comparing it to other state-of-the-art methods, and observe significant improvements in success rates and task execution time.

The study of electron transport properties through a single wall of carbon nanotubes serves as a foundation for a comprehensive investigation of their use in innovative semiconductor technology, enabling the efficient creation of high-frequency oscillators and highly sensitive detectors. A key aspect of this research focuses on how to select the ideal material for radio-frequency gate electrodes in order to enhance the mobility of charge carriers within the channel. Through computational modeling, we demonstrate that the frequency mobility of the gate has a direct correlation with the energy difference between the conduction band edge and the energy level associated with the gate, and we highlight the significance of accurately calculating this energy difference in order to ensure optimal device performance. Furthermore, we have developed a statistical protocol to estimate this energy difference from conductance measurements, and we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using simulations of a radio-frequency gate in contact with a single carbon nanotube. Additionally, we have investigated the transport characteristics of full nanotube field-effect transistors subject to a radio-frequency gate, and we have analyzed how the gate frequency and amplitude influence the mobility of the transport carriers. Importantly, our research has identified the parameters for operating the gate that maximize carrier mobility, and we have shown that the optimal conditions involve a gate frequency and amplitude that is synchronized at twice the frequency of the gate. Finally, we have investigated the influence of temperature on the transport characteristics of these gate materials, and we have identified the parameters for operating the gate that maximize carrier mobility at varying temperatures.

We investigated how the presence of small errors in a system affects the group synchronization of coupled oscillators. This system consists of two groups of nodes with nodes in one group connected in a ring, while nodes in the other group have connections to all others. We found that the stability of the group synchronization can be preserved for large data sets even with minor errors if certain conditions on the system's parameters are met. Additionally, we found that this stability can be enhanced by adjusting these parameters. Our study highlights the importance of system design in achieving group synchronization.

Our study examines the blocking of YouTube by search engines in the European Union. Between November 2022 and January 2023, we conducted research on the top search engines in six EU countries. During this period, a day-after method was employed, where a search query with 'YouTube' was made, and the presence of YouTube in the search outcomes was noted. Our results show that all searched outputs from Western search engines lacked YouTube. Additionally, we made repeated searches from December 2022 to June 2023. Our findings indicate that YouTube remains blocked in the search outcomes. Our initial hypothesis suggested that YouTube would be blocked in some non-dominant search engines but not in leading ones. However, our subsequent data shows that YouTube's absence persists across all searched outputs, including those from dominant search engine providers. Our study's Western search engine blocking data is now consistent with that of Google, where YouTube's URL has been blocked since October 2022. We did not find any search outcomes with YouTube from Eastern search engines. Our analysis suggests that YouTube's blocking may be a gradual process in the EU or that it is being implemented in a targeted manner by Google.

When we apply a $\beta$-function to a system with a general monodromy defect, its behavior differs from that of its defect-free counterpart. To analyze this change, we investigate the system's expansion around its ultraviolet cutoff and represent the resulting series in a form that reveals its spectral properties. By doing so, we're able to determine how the system's eigenvalues respond to an increase in momentum, which in turn allows us to derive the $\beta$-function that governs this interaction. As a concrete example, we consider a specific defect in a two-dimensional topological order framework and show how its behavior correlates with well-known $\beta$-function formulas from the 2D topological central charge models.

We establish that for a cubic Galois field extension K over Q, and a 13-order rational point P in E(K), a specific elliptic curve definition is unique up to a finite number of possibilities. This rationale relies heavily on the underlying theory of Hilbert modular forms.

We explore the effects of network delay on small groups of agents within a distributed protocol. By analyzing the scalar linear systems, we identify distinct operation modes following the implementation of delay and establish a criterion for each mode. These operation modes are classified into five categories, each corresponding to a different regime: (1) negligible delay, (2) low but non-negligible delay, (3) transient regime characterized by oscillations, (4) stabilization, and (5) explosive growth. Furthermore, we investigate how these operation modes can be utilized to implement basic arithmetic operations on group elements, such as addition, multiplication, and exponentiation. Specifically, we demonstrate that by triggering a transition from the stabilization mode to the explosive growth mode at an appropriately chosen time, an estimator can accurately calculate the logarithm of a product of group elements. Additionally, by leveraging the ability to control and combine basic operations, we design and demonstrate a protocol for securely sharing a secret among multiple entities in the presence of a malicious adversary.

Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks often utilizes node labeling to enhance model performance, but conventional pseudo-labeling methods have been shown to decrease model effectiveness beyond a certain point. This study introduces a new labeling technique inspired by self-training and incorporates it into existing models. By combining labeling with the model's initial parameters, this method offers a valuable strategy for graph neural networks. The research demonstrates the benefits of this technique by examining different labeling techniques and the impact of varying label quality on node labeling schemes. Ultimately, the findings highlight the significance of considering label quality and the utility of combining labeling with the model's initial settings.

Our research introduces PatchNet, a versatile and efficient neural network model specifically designed for patch-based video object detection tasks. By leveraging explicit spatial convolutions and incorporating a novel attention mechanism, PatchNet outperforms state-of-the-art approaches while efficiently utilizing computational resources, including a significant 2.8 times gain in FLOPs over MobileNetV2. Additionally, PatchNet's architecture is adaptable to various applications such as video action recognition and human pose estimation, making it a universally applicable model.

We investigated multi-point distribution in a discrete time TASEP with multiple initial configurations, including both random and structured settings. These initial structures allowed us to analyze specific, non-random configurations. Building upon existing research, we extended the findings of 'Asymptotic multi-point distribution in the discrete time TASEP' by considering more complex, multi-point scenarios across various time points, including the long run. Our results demonstrate how the distribution at a given time affects its predecessors. Notably, for random starting points, we showed that the observed data aligns with the predicted statistics from the FEVE model. In contrast, for certain random initial conditions, we found that the tail statistics remain random and uncorrelated at large times. Additionally, examining specific initial structures enabled us to expand our understanding to include more tailored statistics. These findings shed new light on the underlying dynamics of the TASEP model.

Future energy-autonomous base stations will incorporate Switched Radio Frequency (RF) signals and Switching Energy Harvesting (SEH) technology to meet growing wireless demands while minimizing energy consumption. A new general antenna-switching technique is introduced to enhance energy efficiency and guarantee outages in RF-powered networks. The proposed method allows for the simultaneous activation of antennas and RF carriers to maximize energy collection from users. We formulate an optimal power allocation and RF configuration problem subject to constraints on antenna usage, RF modes, and QoS requirements and develop an efficient algorithm based on iterative block confidence propagation to minimize long-term power consumption. The proposed solution effectively balances practical implementation and mathematical complexity, and through simulation, we demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches in achieving low overall power consumption.

We've developed a rigorous mathematical framework for perturbation theory in SU(N) fermion systems. Our approach uses a systematic expansion in (g^2/N) and matches second-order results but surpasses them, achieving accurate third-order derivatives of the Heisenberg matrix. Notably, while third-order Heisenberg matrix derivatives can be computed analytically for SU(2) and SU(3), our method allows for the numerical evaluation of fourth-order derivatives. Our results are in line with Lefshetz involution principles and demonstrate the importance of correcting a flaw in the standard perturbation framework.

In optomechanics, incorporating quantum effects is crucial. The introduction of quantum mechanics was pivotal in the development of this field, but we question whether the standard approach is truly necessary. The typical quantum method treats single photons and single phonons, but real-world applications involve numerous photons and phonons. When occupation numbers are substantial, it's logical to use classical physics to model the system, but this would mean forfeiting the benefits of quantum mechanics. The purpose of this research is to verify if the standard quantum approach is indeed necessary. The study demonstrates that the quantum method is essential, but only under specific conditions. The most significant contribution of this work is the development of an innovative procedure for extracting classical models from quantum descriptions. The technique is versatile and can be applied beyond optomechanics, making it a valuable tool for other areas of physics where quantum and classical states coexist.

On the nonclassical Sobolev space with weight $|x|^\beta \exp(-|x|^7)$, we investigate the direct and embedded spectra of the $j$-th derivative operator on this space, denoted as $J^{(j)}$. Our analysis specifically considers the cases of $j = 1, 2, 3$ and $j = 4$ with the weight changing to $\gamma = \frac{2}{3} \beta$. Our findings concerning the $L^2$-essential spectra have some surprising connections with the generalized sextic Freud weight. For the second operator, we determine the embedded spectrum, while the existence of its compact perturbation determines the embedded spectrum of the third operator. Furthermore, we outline the potential research into the embedded spectrum of the fourth operator.

A wall-following robot's path can be influenced by its field of view and sensing capabilities. We are studying how these factors impact a robot's performance, with a goal of developing an optimal sensing distance for image-based navigation. By utilizing simulated scenarios and a generated database of virtual trajectories, we evaluated the impact of sensing distance on robot trajectory. Our results indicate that increased sensing distance can result in higher deviation from the optimal path, and we identify scenarios in which a robot with a wide field of view may deviate more from the optimal path compared to a robot with a narrow field of view.

This paper focuses on the perturbative algebraic quantum field theory from Dowker and Mc-Cormack (1974), with a view to understanding the nature of its elements as they relate to a chosen Cauchy surface. We centre our analysis on the restrictions applied to the field operators as they interact with this surface. A key aspect of our investigation involves identifying the subalgebras formed by limiting sets of field operators. These operator sets are confined to regions within a slice of four-dimensional spacetime, called a Cauchy surface. A significant finding emerges when we consider multiple choices for the Cauchy surface, leading us to conclude that its selection variably defines the subalgebras and thus the elements of the theory. We use the example of a free scalar field to illustrate these observations in detail.

Recent advancements in convolutional neural networks have led to impressive performance gains, but their adapted multi-classature learning often results in compromised accuracy and overlapping feature sets between classes. In response, we introduce a novel smoke-detection framework that addresses these issues and outperforms prior research. By initially distinguishing smoke and non-smoke images using a novel noise-aware autoencoder, we isolate class-specific features and prevent overlapping. Subsequently, a class-scale adaptive pooling module enables the model to extract unique features from each class, preventing feature mimicry. Our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Smoke2K dataset, demonstrating a 4% improvement in accuracy and increased robustness to noise and augmentation.

This research investigates the design of robust, multi-qubit quantum gates in ion chains called Molmer-Sorensen gates, specifically focusing on its robustness to frequency variations. We developed a method to analyze the frequency robustness of these gates and discovered that a particular arrangement, the helical design, significantly reduces systematic errors compared to a linear ion chain. In the helical design, the distance between ions increases gradually from center to periphery. We found that the center ions can be made virtually immune to frequency-related errors by optimizing this arrangement, improving entanglement accumulation and quantum state preparation. Additionally, we explored the trade-offs between robustness, entanglement accumulation, and quantum state preparation by adjusting the ion spacing in the helical design.

Our study employs first-principles calculations to examine the structural behavior
of perovskite ferroelectrics. We investigated the equilibrium structure, phonons
and Born effective parameters of BaTiO$_3$ with different A-cations of varying
size. The results reveal a correlation between the equilibrium volume, A-cation
size, and B-cation displacement. Additionally, we found that the spontaneous polarization
is sensitive to the Born effective parameters, but also depends on the strain and bond
lengths, particularly those related to the A-cation. These findings are expected to
enhance our understanding of the ferroelectric behavior in these materials.

Multivariate Gaussian processes can be utilized in various applications such as modeling, forecasting, and optimization by assuming certain dependencies between processes, even if data is scarce. Recent breakthroughs have made high-dimensional data analysis more feasible, even at the linear scale. Previously, Kernels for multivariate Gaussian processes were limited, but research now offers new, compact representations for maintaining statistical correlations. We introduce the multivariate matrix variance kernel, which can effectively model complex dependencies between processes. We demonstrate the kernel's capability to ensure conditional independence between processes in a graphical model, even at non-linear scales. The kernel can be utilized in Gaussian process regression and other methods such as optimization and modeling. The kernel's efficiency is particularly beneficial when data is scarce, as it can effectively handle high-dimensional data.

Our proposed model, the Recurrent Quantum Circuit using Spatially-Adjacent Recurrences (R-COHER), integrates multiple quantum circuit learning approaches to efficiently solve quantum many-body problems. By leveraging the structural properties of recurrent neural networks, we enhance the coherence of quantum states and improve the performance of ground state estimators. Our results show that R-COHER outperforms existing methods in computing molecular ground states, achieving high accuracy while maintaining a lower error tolerance for a given Fidelity. Additionally, R-COHER exhibits superior energy scaling efficiency compared to prior methods, and our experiments indicate that it has potential applications in larger quantum systems, potentially surpassing the capabilities of more traditional approaches, such as the Quantum Neural Tangent Kernel.

A new method called the Generalized Chebyshev method is introduced, which uses polynomial interpolation to efficiently optimize objective functions. By leveraging the smoothness of functions, the method achieves superior average-case performance compared to gradient descent, while ensuring fast convergence on a fixed function class. The method's applicability is demonstrated in enhanced Newton-Raphson methods for computing the square root and integral operators, and in a stochastic optimization algorithm outperforming stochastic gradient descent.

Research has been focused on the optical properties of interlayer excitons within twisted heterostructures composed of layered materials with moiré patterns. Studies, however, have not adequately explained the observed interlayer exciton state at low-energies through theoretical analysis. We developed a model that describes the primary low-energies optical spectra in these structures by accounting for both intralayer and interlayer excitons. The interlayer exciton contribution, significant at low-energies, is contingent on the exciton binding energy, which we estimate to be approximately 10 meV, by referencing earlier research and calculations. The optical transition matrix elements are determined based on the moiré pattern orbital structure, while the interlayer exciton Hamiltonian is inferred from observed near-zero-energies excitonic states. The resulting spectra, calculated through a combined density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory approach, showcase the prominence of interlayer excitons at low-energies. We demonstrate that the interlayer exciton contribution can be modified by applying an external gate to alter the interlayer separation. The proposed theoretical framework offers an efficient approach for predicting the optical properties of interlayer excitons in various moiré heterostructures.

This study investigates adaptive algorithms for positioning and tracking a mobile entity within changing environments, focusing on adaptive probabilistic data association algorithms and their application to multi-agent tracking. Our analysis reveals that an algorithm designed for a single target can effectively solve the multi-target tracking problem, yielding superior performance, particularly in uncertain situations, and enhancing estimation accuracy. Moreover, we demonstrate that this algorithm is capable of handling a critical parameter through self-adjustment, thus simplifying implementation and operation. Simulation results validate the performance advantages of our proposed approach.

We present direct measurements of the helicity angles and polarization properties of $W^{\pm}$ bosons and $Z$ boson production, conducted using the CMS detector at the LHC, with data collected in 2017 and 2018, at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy. The studied phenomena involve collisions of protons with leading $p_T$ values of 35 GeV or higher, where the $W$ or $Z$ boson is identified in one of the decay channels involving electrons or muons. The measured values of helicity fractions and angles do not deviate from standard model predictions, while the observed polarization parameters appear to be in line with theoretical expectations for similar $pp$ collisions.

A new approach to a non-compact, flat spacetime's holographic boundary is developed by incorporating a non-compact version of the Einstein-Hilbert action's bulk boundary term into the action. In this framework, an novel phase for both repulsive and attractive gravity scenarios is introduced and found to be analogous to the original phase in the AdS case. By focusing solely on the Cotton tensor as the indicator of the vacuum state, a complete generalisation of the flat spacetime's Wick rotation from AdS spacetime is achieved. Furthermore, both new and original phases exhibit dual descriptions by conformal boundary theories, which are proven to be equivalent. In both scenarios, the bulk action's diffeomorphism invariance translates to the conformal boundary's conformal symmetry. In the flat spacetime case, an additional mechanism is discovered to maintain this invariance.

We establish that orthomodular lattices and orthomodular spaces share an equivalent concept. This connection allows us to view any orthomodular space as a representation of an orthomodular lattice. Furthermore, the first-order language derived from this framework has the capability to express the principles governing quantum trace-preserving state transitions, as outlined in the quantum pigeonhole principle.

In abstract reasoning, a strategy involves comparing sets of attributes within a problem statement to prove relationships between entities. Researchers have recently created a symbolic framework for representing and generalizing such reasoning, which involves first-person statements with multiple entities and attributes. While this framework can facilitate human-like thinking, a significant obstacle remains in acquiring knowledge represented in this format. Unlike existing AI systems, there's a notable gap in how these models learn, between what's typical (e.g. through reinforcement learning) and what's desired (through explicit rewards for making progress). Our solution to this challenge is an auxiliary learning system that uses a neural network to process human-generated proof diagrams and translate them into the required attribute-value logic representations. These generated proof representations can then be used to provide explicit rewards to the primary learning system. As such, this is an example of a transfer learning scenario. Our experiments with this setup demonstrate significant improvements to the review process. Specifically, our system was evaluated by comparing it to a typical reinforcement learning setup where the attribute-value logic representation is learned directly, and the results show that it leads to a notable increase in the number of successful attributes. This, in turn, indicates that the auxiliary learning system is effective in preparing the attribute-value logic representations and, through the proof representations, enhancing the learning process.

We derive an expression for $2k-1$th moments of $\mathfrak{S} f$ and $\mathfrak{S}^2 f$ where $k \geq 2$, given that $f$ is a real primitive cuspidal function, leveraging Watson's formula, Soundararajan and Harper's moments of $L$ functions under the Riemann Hypothesis, and a particular series expansion.

Preconditioners for interior point methods typically involve an inner iteration
terminating criterion based on sufficient decrease. This study examines enhancing
preconditioners' efficiency by introducing an early termination option for the
inner iteration. Specifically, this option involves terminating the inner
iteration as soon as the criterion is met, rather than completing a predetermined
number of iterations, for each individual preconditioning step. The study
investigates whether this approach extension yields significant performance gains
and evaluates its effects on the overall interior point method using numerical tests.

We need the transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$, which describes how a heavy quark pairs with $N$-flavor light quarks in the variable flavor number scheme, to derive renormalization group equations for the latter. By assuming an ansatz based on renormalization group properties and matching conditions, we propose an expression for $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ and demonstrate that it meets the required criteria. Specifically, our analysis verifies that the proposed transition function yields the correct results for $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N=1)$ and $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N=5)$. Furthermore, our formula exhibits behavior in line with perturbative QCD for all $N$ flavors.

We've launched the AI Incident Database, a central hub for documenting incidents related to intelligent systems, and we're calling on the community to contribute. As the field continues to grow, we need a framework for sharing knowledge about incidents that have occurred during AI development and deployment. This database will serve as a resource for informing guidelines and best practices in resilient and trustworthy AI. Contribute by sharing your experiences at https://incidentcatalog.com/submissions.

A revised version of the Einstein-Yang-Mills equations is introduced as an extension of Einstein's general relativity and Yang-Mills theory. The model builds upon prior research by Deser, Teitelboim, and Hansen and is reinterpreted through a modified curvature tensor, as initially suggested by Hehl and coworkers. We examine the revised Yang-Mills sector in a flat spacetime backdrop and propose an extension of the model known as the 'expanded revised Yang-Mills theory.' The new theory is based on an erg differential equation, aiming to preserve gauge invariance. We demonstrate that by incorporating gauge invariance into the erg differential equation, it mimics the behavior of the Yang-Mills equation. Furthermore, we show that although pure Yang-Mills theory does not yield stable solutions, we can force compatibility with Yang-Mills theory by imposing additional restrictions. We then dilute our findings to yield a revised Proca theory, yielding stable solutions, and ultimately use our model as a foundation for interpreting gravitational spin in general relativity. Our analysis indicates that gravitational spin amounts to one-third of a unit spin.

To address a monitoring system's capability to resolve conflicts between several processes running under different specifications, a advanced model checking technique has been created. This technique checks if a particular run of a set of programs conforms to multiple specifications by translating the run into a graph and translating each specification into a set of graph constraints. Then, using model checking capabilities, the system checks if the graph meets the specifications by solving the resulting constraint satisfaction problem. This technique is capable of detecting both process violations and conflicting situations between different processes, and it can even identify the source of the conflict. An example demonstration shows how this technique helps monitor a set of air traffic control procedures.

Protocols for quantum information processing need to preserve the unique characteristics of quantum states in order to function correctly. Currently used protocols, however, clone quantum states in order to perform certain operations, which is undesirable. A previously developed protocol, QUIPPER, was modified to maintain its state cloning limitations, resulting in Proto-Quipper-M. While maintaining the cloning limitations of quantum states in Proto-Quipper-M, it was discovered that universal quantum computation is possible with only a single auxiliary qubit available for use in the process.

We analyze the largest eigenvalue of the sum of a 3x3 random matrix from the ensembles of GOE, GUE, and GSE, and apply the principle of finite-size scaling to effectively examine the statistical properties at the thermodynamic limit. The results are further validated by comparing the findings with those obtained using a $1/\sqrt{\beta}$ scaling criterion in random matrix theory.

We investigate the possibility of leveraging two-mode squeezing as a resource in quantum-enhanced observation of an optical phase. Theoretical considerations indicate that in a network of connected optical nodes, two-mode squeezing can be implemented through a single light pulse, incorporating all relevant nodes. This process can be realized by initially preparing a state with high Fock components and then applying a suitable beam splitter interaction. The resulting two-mode squeezing will enable further advancements in quantum-based techniques for phase measurement and optical circuit connectivity.

One of the most difficult problems in computationally solving the NP-complete partitioning challenge is multiway number partitioning. On the other hand, partitioning homologous chromosomes in eukaryotic organisms with multiple sets of chromosomes is relatively straightforward. We propose a conceptually simple and efficient algorithm for generating all feasible chromosomal configurations based on a binary representation of each chromosome. We then adapt this concept to efficiently solve multiway number partitioning by reducing it to the chromosomal configuration problem. This adaptation enables us to take advantage of advanced techniques developed for binary constraint satisfaction problems, thereby outperforming existing methods for solving multiway number partitioning.

A new modified logistic equation with delay is suggested to improve a previous model by Li and Smith (2021), whose positive solution converges to a positive equilibrium in a spatially homogeneous state, suitable for modeling single-cell populations. It is demonstrated that, unlike the original equation, this modified model always reaches a positive equilibrium in any given spatially homogeneous initial condition. Furthermore, through numerical simulations, it is shown that, similar to the original equation, this modified model exhibits the same characteristics of temporarily non-homogeneous cell distributions and eventual convergence to a uniform population.

Background
Highly branched trees have wide applications in various fields such as phylogenetics, computer science, and physics. Their geometry can be described using the following parameters: tree age, branch lengths, and a unique symmetry associated with each node called the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation. This study focuses on point processes where events occur along tree branches with associated event times, offering the potential to incorporate time information. Our analysis measures the limiting ratios of events under the ILR transformation, determining their distribution and low frequency asymptotics. This framework allows us to compare event times across different branches, taking into account variations in branch lengths and tree age. Our results demonstrate that the ILR transformation significantly enhances event time analysis, overcoming significant limitations when branch lengths are uniform. When branch lengths differ, the ILR transformation reveals distinct patterns, uncovering unique insights that were previously inaccessible.

In hybrid quantum conductors, a key concept is entangled Cooper pairs, 
within which both wave function position and momentum are undefined. 
As an important application of this concept, the entanglement of these pairs 
can be utilized to generate non-local spin-singlet states necessary for 
efficient quantum computation.  We have developed a theoretical model that 
describes how this process occurs during a drive-electron process and how the 
entanglement affects it, with a notable influence of spin-orbit coupling and 
Heisenberg exchange interactions.  As a result, the entanglement not only 
facilitates the generation of spin-singlet states, but also enhances their 
quantum levels due to a difference in phase shift induced by the spin-orbit 
coupling.  This phenomenon has the potential to be observed through measurement 
using a scanning tunneling microscope to study mesoscopic hybrid quantum conductors.

Researchers used the DRIS facility at CEA/IRAMIS for in-depth nuclear research, combining data from proton-induced gamma-ray spectroscopy and beta-decay studies. A high-accuracy nuclear structure investigation of 62-66 Ge and 61-65 Ni nuclei across a wide range of excitation energies was conducted, allowing for comparisons with 58 Ni, 59 Cu, 60 Zn, 61 Ga, and 62 Zn reference points. Our research focused on the nuclear shell model, long-range two-body interactions, and the collective characteristics of these nuclei, revealing their properties in detail. Key findings included the phase transition from the nickel nuclear structure to that of geranium around N = 40, the increase in triaxial 0-neutron particle-hole vortex components with growing Z and N, and the emergence of collective characteristics in nuclei far from stability, which was predicted by models and confirmed by experiments. Our study also allowed for the extraction of primary proton and neutron two-body interactions, enabling the comparison of extracted interaction with established data and suggesting its extension to new nuclei, 58 Ni, 59 Cu, 60 Zn, 61 Ga, and 62 Zn. Moreover, our research indicated that second-order corrections to the weak interaction could account for the n-p asymmetry observed in nature, which might be valid for a wide range of nuclei.

Researchers utilized the $B\\otimes$-IMS method at the ISOLDE-CSNS facility at CERN to analyze the decay properties of several short-lived, neutron-poor nuclei. The study focused on measuring the ground state branching ratios of $^{64}$Ge, $^{66}$Ge, $^{67}$Ge, and $^{68}$Ge by separating their ionized particles through the $B\\otimes$-IMS device in conjunction with the Boekelmann detector. The results revealed new data for $^{67}$Ge and confirmed previous findings for other, more stable, Ge isotopes. The study showed that the $B\\otimes$-IMS method is an effective tool for analyzing rare, neutron-poor decay products and can be applied to further research in this field.

This study introduces an innovative approach to U(1) gauge theory by leveraging normalizing flows and incorporating gauge symmetries within the model framework. By adding a gauge equivalent prior to training, our method maintains the physical meaning of the generated configurations. We analyze two distinct gauge bases for U(1) and investigate their implications on the learning process. Our proposed technique is applied to various lattice systems, and the results show minimal disruption to the sampling efficiency despite the introduction of gauge equivalences. Notably, in the SU(2) Yang-Mills case, our method enables the separation of infrared and ultraviolet regions in the generated samples, and we demonstrate its utility in the computation of observables such as the magnetic field and the trace of the energy tensor.

This study introduces a versatile text recognition model that's specifically designed to identify and process various forms of structured text, such as addresses, dates, and driver's license numbers. The proposed model is able to recognize a wide range of text patterns, including its associated metadata, like the location on an image where the text was found. The framework can be adapted to recognize different types of structured text patterns, simply by updating the label and pre-trained metadata, without the need for further training. The model outperformed existing benchmark models in several challenging text recognition tasks, while demonstrating improved efficiency in recognizing more complex metadata patterns.

The purpose of this study is to provide an overview of the measurement of the cross-section for the production of top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically for proton-proton collisions with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Data were collected over a period of approximately 9 months, during which 79.2 inverse femtobarns of data were recorded. The focus of this measurement is on the events containing one isolated muon and three jets, where the energy of the muon and the transverse energy of the jets were regulated. The measurement also accounted for the uncertainty associated with the muon isolation, which resulted in a cross-section of 772 ± 6 (stat) ± 17 (sys) ± 6 (theoretical) nanobarns. This measurement is in line with theoretical predictions from the Standard Model, specifically for the next-to-leading order predictions with calculations from next-to-leading order perturbative quantum chromodynamics, where the standard model predicts a cross-section of 828 nanobarns.

Deep reasoning tasks in reasoning-based question answering (RBA) require access to a database, which is not available in certain cases, causing their corresponding Deep Reasoning Networks (DRNs) to fail.
