We evaluate our method on two datasets, ICDAR 2013 and CASIA1R, and achieve improved results compared to existing methods. The source code can be found at https://github.com/arpitdennison/RRR-NER.

Law enforcement and public agencies widely issue identification (ID) cards, often including text on the back that can be difficult to read, even with the aid of an OCR system. This challenge stems from the varied layout and visual content of ID cards, which can differ significantly from one another. Furthermore, the extraction of key information, such as names and dates of birth, depends on accurately parsing the structural elements of the extracted text. In contrast to existing solutions, our proposed method tackles this complex task through a natural language processing (NLP) approach, leveraging pre-trained language models to improve the accuracy of extraction. By employing pre-trained models in this manner, our system demonstrates superior performance on multiple datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results in the process.

This research focuses on channel estimation, particularly in scenarios where there is significant movement. It proposes an innovative approach that utilizes a special type of neural network called a long short-term memory (LSTM) to improve channel estimation accuracy. This method involves creating a trained LSTM module that can effectively remove unwanted noise and obstacles' interference in the signal, leading to more precise data transmission. Results show that this approach significantly enhances channel estimation and overall system performance, even in highly complex environments. Furthermore, LSTM channel estimation exhibits robustness against irregularities in the channel and obstacles' movements, thus ensuring reliable data transmission.

We utilize a advanced hierarchical approach and maximum a posteriori estimation method to restore a single low resolution astronomical image. Our technique effectively implements a non-local means algorithm while accounting for edge information, achieving superior results compared to existing methods. Additionally, we have developed a ground truth based metric to evaluate the performance of image restoration algorithms. Our findings demonstrate that our approach surpasses other established algorithms in terms of accuracy and visual effectiveness, even when applied to images with exceptional level of detail.

We suggest an innovative deep neural network reduction approach where a generated binary neural network is trained end-to-end without any regularization techniques. Since the binary network is inherently resistant to data overfitting due to its reduced model complexity, our approach doesn't require tedious parameter adjustment or ensemble methods. Notably, our end-to-end binary training approach allows the entire model to be adapted simultaneously, which enhances its overall performance. We evaluate the efficacy of this method using the CIFAR-10 and ResNet-18 architecture, comparing its results with existing binary reduction techniques. Our experiments demonstrate that this novel approach yields state-of-the-art performance on these datasets.

In 2018, the European Committee for Future Accelerators established an Early Career Researchers' Panel to represent and consult the global particle physics community regarding its future accelerator-based research and development needs. The panel recently created a survey to gather input from researchers and published a report summarizing the feedback received from more than 2700 respondents, which is being presented in this article.
Graphical representations in this work illustrate concepts rather than provide comprehensive coverage of results.

This study introduces a Federated Learning framework to improve a single entity's ability to understand the actions of multiple interacting humans through multiple robotic platforms. A key challenge in developing this understanding, known as ontologies, is establishing a common reference point to describe and align diverse individual perspectives. Leverage is taken from the established field of concept learning, where algorithms successfully navigate the differences in word meanings across various languages. Our framework relies on the collective input from multiple robotic platforms, each observing a single interacting human, to build a unified ontology. A key innovation is the use of a novel, decentralized process to combine the observations from all robotic platforms, enabling them to understand the actions as a shared, common concept. Successful demonstrations in a controlled environment showed that our approach allows for accurate action-based decision-making, even when there is no prior understanding of the environment or the actions to be executed.

This research introduces a novel estimator that mitigates a prevalent issue in minimum average differentiability estimation, namely that small changes often result in significantly varying estimates. Our approach specifically addresses the problem of maintaining smoothness in the context of efficient semiparametric estimation, and leverages a parametric model combined with random effects to achieve this goal. By contrasting our method with another powerful technique, the Newey-West estimator, we demonstrate its advantages in terms of smoothness while maintaining similar asymptotic performance. Our analysis is complemented by empirical evidence showcasing the proposed estimator's superior properties.

Knowledge graph link prediction has gained significant interest as a task that uses external knowledge to enhance link completion capabilities. Current approaches encode knowledge graphs into a compact representation and utilize neural models to predict missing links. However, these models solely rely on graph structural information, disregarding the valuable knowledge extracted from relation examples that could enhance model performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel KRLP approach, relation-example-augmented neural network (REAN), which incorporates knowledge extracted from relation examples to improve link prediction. REAN's relation-example-augmentation module leverages relation examples to enhance the feature representation of candidate pairs through a linear transformer encoder. We evaluate REAN on three datasets, achieving state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on knowledge graph validation and test sets.

In the context of the Hagedorn phase of thermal QCD, we initially establish the Debye mass types for both pure gauge theory and quark-filled phases at zero baryonic chemical potential. We then extend our analysis to scenarios with a non-zero baryonic chemical potential, comparing magnetic and femto-scale Debye masses. We find that introducing baryonic chemical potential shifts the Debye mass types in a way that depends on whether it pertains to baryons, quarks, or mesons.

We examined the magnetic arrangements of the rare-earth metals Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7, which exhibit similar 5:2 ratios of rare-earth to ruthenium metals, in the hexagonal 0.5-ba2+ compound. Ru1, with an even valence, formed a antiferromagnetic pattern, whereas Ru2, having an odd valence, demonstrated a ferromagnetic arrangement in both substances. In Tb3RuO7, the magnetic dipoles were directed perpendicular to the c-axis, while the spins in Nd3RuO7 were aligned parallel to the c-axis. Furthermore, the oxygen ions in both materials formed a chain of magnetic dipoles pointing in the same direction. Our studies, using polariized synchrotron-radiation XRD, allowed us to assess the magnetic arrangements of these compounds.

Our research introduces an novel, function-based classification method, which classifies signal representations by approximating class decisions through function evaluations at sample points. Unlike typical classification methods that rely on global predictions, our approach utilizes localized classifier functions, facilitating generalization beyond training data points. For one-dimensional signals, we establish a theorem demonstrating the effectiveness of our method for low-dimensional signals. Experimental results across various signal dimensions showcase its efficiency and effectiveness.

In order to resolve issues with limited information about target variables, we propose a new semi-generative model, called the causal network model. This model has two primary components: a probabilistic model that represents causes and a probabilistic model that represents effects. Unlike traditional generative models, which assume the target variable can be generated from its causes, the causal network model posits that the target variable can only influence its effects, thereby addressing the one-way relationship between causes and effects. We examine the relationship between the causal network model and its variational approximations, and discuss how this model can be applied in various domains, such as modeling disease progression and intervention analysis. We also propose an option for handling continuous target variables, and provide an example of how the model can be used to analyze data from clinical trials.

Recent advancements in deep learning have largely been driven by the widespread adoption of neural networks. Despite decades of research, the underlying geometric structure of these models remains poorly understood. We believe that revealing the intrinsic geometry of deep learning models could lead to more effective and transferable algorithms and new, high-performance architectural frameworks. In this study, we delve into the geometric properties of neural networks from multiple perspectives, and conclude by exploring how exploring this geometry may unlock novel applications within continued neural network development.

Consider a cubic field of discriminant $d$ and let the integer sequence $\{b_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ be defined as the sequence of radicands for its lattice minima, with the exception of $b_0 = 1$. We establish in this paper that there exist arbitrarily large values of $d$ for which the sequence $\{b_n(d)\}_{n\geq 0}$ does not become regular, meaning its norm does not repeat for any $n>0$. Additionally, we prove that for any given $b_0=1$, there exist an infinitely abundant supply of cubic fields in which their associated lattice minima sequences do not exhibit regular norms.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit challenging-to-interpretable predictions due to their lack of transparency. Analyzing DNNs becomes even more complicated as their sizes increase, making prediction interpretation more difficult. In response to this, a novel algorithm called layerwise relevance propagation (LRP) was developed to facilitate the detailed interpretation of DNNs. LRP is an efficient approach that requires no additional parameters or training beyond the original model. While it has been successfully applied to shallow networks, adapting it for deep networks remains a complex task. In this paper, a new framework is proposed to facilitate the interpretation of large DNNs through feature selection and removal of irrelevant components. The proposed framework was tested on DNNs and proven to be more efficient in reducing computational costs without compromising its accuracy. The framework's effectiveness was verified on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ICDAR7 datasets through comparative analysis with the original DNNs.

The $\mathcal{S}_{r}(n)$ represents r-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, which are part of a broader mathematical concept. These numbers, denoted by $\mathcal{S}_{r}(n)$, can be seen as a combination of classical Stirling numbers of the second kind, with the parameter $r$ influencing their structure. For $r \geq 2$, a recursive formula is developed to determine $\mathcal{S}_{r}(n)$. Furthermore, the focus is on finding a explicit formula for $\mathcal{S}_{r}(n)$ when $r \geq 2$. Notably, when $r = 2$, the expression aligns with existing Stirling numbers of the second kind. Additionally, a relationship between $\mathcal{S}_{r}(n)$ and ${n-1 \choose n-r}$ is established through combinatorial evidence.

We introduce a new method to categorize domains within any given layered material by employing
group theory, specifically considering the symmetry of domain walls. Our analysis reveals that
the total number of possible domains across all layered materials is finite and can be determined
theoretically. We develop a systematic approach to categorize and study domain classifications within
any given layered material, applying this method to well-known materials and identifying unclassified
domains in the Materials Project database. Furthermore, we develop a relationship between domain
classifications and the symmetries within material families. Our findings enable comprehensive
comparisons between the theoretical number of domain classifications and the total number listed in the
Materials Project database, showing that there are still many undiscovered domain classifications in these
materials that need to be studied and categorized.

We examine the relationship between spatial and momentum states on a general, high-dimensional space called a manifold. Its geometric properties allow us to pinpoint a maximum amount of detail in both position and momentum realms, with the latter tied to the de-Broglie wavelength. This discovery helps us visualize how a quantum system behaves in a space with its own geometric properties, analogous to compactification in String Theory. We show that these relationships give rise to discrete, grainy aspects in both position and momentum spaces, with the coarseness tied to the wavelength. This understanding enables us to deduce how the system behaves over time and with multiple systems interacting and we find that these conditions lead to the development of non-local, interconnected phenomena.

We introduce an improved simulation method for Monte Carlo simulations by utilizing complex-valued affine coupling layers. Our novel approach employs Gaussian complexes, which comprise complex-valued affine transformations, along with complex-valued invertible layers like parameterized orthogonal matrices. This method can be implemented using exclusively real-valued computations via division of the simulation into real and imaginary components. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that the deterministic part of the simulation can be efficiently implemented while its stochastic component still maintains a significant degree of randomness, comparable to the standard Gaussian flow method. Additionally, we provide theoretical proof of the method's correctness and convergence.

We introduce a novel model incorporating $\text{U(1)}_{\text{F}}$ flavor symmetry breaking to address the disparity between the top and bottom quark masses, as well as their flavor conservation. We demonstrate that the electroweak $\text{U(1)}_{\varphi}$ symmetry, which generates the Higgs potential, is preserved by all fermions except for the three up-type quarks. Upon acquiring a vacuum expectation value, the $\text{U(1)}_{\text{F}}$ symmetry is broken, resulting in the introduction of diquark condensates as well as unusual flavor-violating interactions among gauge bosons and Higgs bosons. We analyze the phenomenological implications of this model on diquark physics, flavor-violating boson interactions, and dark matter candidates in this model.

This paper investigates the utilization of virtual private networks, particularly virtual private network tunnels, by malicious entities to conceal their activities online. It is established that malicious individuals employ VPNs in order to shield their identities and create anonymity. Consequently, these malicious activities often take place within hidden networks, making it difficult for law enforcement to detect and track them. Notably, attacks perpetrated via VPNs predominantly target online services and monetary transactions. This study aims to identify and analyze the behaviors characteristic of malicious entities utilizing VPNs, and to differentiate them from legitimate VPN users. For this purpose, a method of attribute analysis was developed, and data from a VPN provider were examined. The results indicate that malicious entities exhibit distinct attributes in comparison to legitimate VPN users, including, amongst others, a greater likelihood of engaging in spamming, purchasing items from darknet e-commerce platforms, and engaging in money laundering. Furthermore, it was observed that malicious entities tend to create and sell their own malware, and use automated tools to enhance their chances of success. The research reveals that utilizing attribute analysis based on an individual's overall behavior often fails to accurately identify malicious entities, as this approach can be deceiving due to overfitting. In contrast, using a behavior-based approach that considers multiple features and incorporating expert knowledge helps to enhance identification accuracy. The findings suggest that attributing malicious behavior to VPN users is often associated with their geographical location, and that regions with higher online malicious activity rates tend to have a greater presence of malicious VPN users.

The rapid evolution of large language models has led to a growing trend of adapting them to diverse new languages, rather than training entirely new models, in order to support high-efficiency, high-quality language understanding tasks in under-resourced languages. Despite the abundance of research on adapting language models, there is a noticeable lack of systematic evaluations and analyses of their adaptability to new languages. In this study, we develop and apply a comprehensive framework for evaluating language model adaptability and conduct a thorough investigation of its components, findings. Our work offers insights into what factors influence the adaptability of language models and provides practical guidelines for selecting suitable language models and adaptation methods for a given language. Additionally, we collect and make publicly available a large and representative dataset of 292 hours, comprising 15 million samples, drawn from 19 low-resource languages, to facilitate future research in this area.

Researchers created collapsing rotating cores with rotating velocities between 0.42f and 0.64f, with a ratio of specific rotation $\beta$ varying accordingly, where f is the critical rotation velocity. Such cores had two embedded energy reservoirs: a central protostar with varying mass and a surrounding disc. With a disc mass fraction of 0.1898, they found that the protostar's mass was directly proportional to its kinetic energy relative to gravitational energy. Furthermore, the kinetic energy in the disc was shown to be directly proportional to its mass. Its kinetic energy represented about 42% of its gravitational energy, similar to that of the protostar. Using the Eddington prescription, they found that the protostar's radius was determined solely by its surface gravity, supporting the protostar model's stability. Modeling a disc with decreasing angular velocity and temperature towards the core allowed them to apply the Shields criterion, discovering that lower-mass cores were more susceptible to binary formation. With increasing mass, the core's central region's Kelvin-Helmholtz time exceeded its rotational period, leading to the elimination of binary formation. Observing a binary mass trend of approximately $M_{bin} \sim M_{\ast}^{1.3}$, with increasing thermal diffusion, they found that the binary mass increased. Utilizing a more efficient three-dimensional radiative-hydrodynamic model, they replicated their previous findings, demonstrating the compatibility of their models with observations.

The m-ar-K function represents a modified version of the traditional ar-K function, widely employed in dimensionality reduction applications. Recent research revealed that its matrix form offers more efficient storage capabilities than other similar methods. In this study, we introduce an improved algorithm for calculating the m-ar-K function, enhancing computational speed by approximately five times. Additionally, we have created a software implementation available online at https://github.com/romanov-ds/marK/tree/main/algorithms/huber_optimization.

A proposed EPC (Extended Pushdown Computation) model, which incorporates a register machine with a potentially unbounded large integer, may offer a new perspective on the interplay between CPT (Computation by Turing Machine in a Countable Model) and PTIME (Pseudo-Nilpotence Time). If a super-polynomial EPC bound can be established, it could imply that CPT is not efficiently equivalent to PTIME. Nevertheless, demonstrating even a linear EPC bound remains an open challenge.

A ring is $\sigma$-idealistic if its collection of ideals forms a $\sigma$-ideal when combined (possibly infinitely many sums). We classify such rings based on whether every ideal is elementary, and establish that in a $\sigma$-idealistic ring with all ideals being elementary, any ideal formed by taking finite sums of these elementary ideals is also elementary. Additionally, we explore the inverse of this statement.

Recent years have witnessed a surge in the amount of data being shared via social media platforms like Twitter, Instagram, and Facebook. As a result, users are exposed to an overwhelming number of narratives daily, gained from either friends, family, or influential figures. Furthermore, individuals are beginning to use these social media platforms not only to share personal experiences but also to engage in informed decision-making, particularly in political environments. Consequently, the number of misinformed voters has reached alarming levels, potentially influencing critical elections. To address this issue, we propose Identifying Narratives, a graph-based method that can help users to make more informed choices by pinpointing and disseminating true stories. Our approach leverages the structure of a user's social network to establish a friendship graph, where each edge is weighted according to the degree of connection between individuals, and then applies a community detection algorithm to identify clusters of closely linked friends. Furthermore, we develop a narrative representation that can adapt to various levels of user influence and use techniques such as the Bayesian Affinity Scalable Algorithm and Modularity Maximization to pin down true stories within each group, and show the effectiveness of our method through simulation experiments.

This research proposes an event detection system capable of accurately processing events occurring at varying spatial resolutions. A novel approach utilizes a hierarchical structure of Convolutional Neural Networks to analyze video footage both spatially and temporally, with a focus on distinguishing between internal and external camera perspectives. Equipped with a camera angle invariance module, this system can withstand differences in camera orientation. Furthermore, a modified Camera Intrusion Detection System is integrated to enhance security. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our event detection model through experimental evaluation using the Segmentation of Salient Human Body Parts dataset.

We present a joint analysis of $abacusLens$ stage IV CMB lensing predictions and the galaxy survey $VSA$ measurements of mass power spectrum and redshift distribution. CMB lensing provides a reliable early data set, while $VSA$ serves as a test case due to its smaller volume and potential bias. We investigate multiple galaxy bias models and examine how their parameters affect mass power spectrum measurements. Our results reveal constraints on the mass-to-radius ratio, with a $1-\sigma$ uncertainty of $1.1\times10^{-3}$, and parameters related to redshift distribution, constrained within a $10-20\%$ margin. This analysis highlights the value of combining CMB lensing and galaxy data for obtaining more accurate and mixed cosmological parameter constraints at lower redshift.

Deep neural networks have achieved immense success in various applications. 
However, their reliance on large amounts of data makes their reliability and trustworthiness questionable in high-stakes situations. 
The requirement for substantial data also hampers their implementation by organizations with restricted resources. 
This study proposes a pioneering framework, named Adversarial Sample Generation through Randomized Lagrangian Method, which generates robust models capable of withstanding extreme perturbations while utilizing minimal data. 
The framework works by optimizing a Lagrangian function with randomized constraints to produce counterexamples that enhance the model's robustness. 
Through theoretical analysis and experimental results, we demonstrate the model's capability to withstand significant perturbations at par with state-of-the-art models that require much larger datasets. 
Notably, our model requires only 10\% the data required by the comparative models, thereby significantly reducing its training data needs. 
The framework shows exceptional performance in both linear and nonlinear regression applications.

To capture rapid changes in rumors dynamics, a new time series task is introduced, namely, time series classification using the popular TDistributed Optimally Weighted Multiple Linear Regression method. Three datasets are created by varying the dependent variable, choosing between location information and precursor features, leading to distinct models. A comprehensive evaluation follows, where different models are compared across datasets, and the influence of feature selection on classification results is examined. Notably, models are found to perform optimally when location information precedes features, as predicted, with location affecting the peak and decline of rumors more significantly than features.

A comprehensive investigation into several well-known dimensionality reduction techniques and their effectiveness at preserving relevant information for hyperspectral pixel classification is presented in this study. Multiple feature extraction methods, including Uninformative Variable Elimination and informative variable selection, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA, RBC, Riesz Transform, t-SNE, LLGA, ICA, and LLE, were employed to examine their influence on hyperspectral pixel signals. Utilizing two benchmark datasets and the Hybrid Hybrid Support Vector Machine classifier, the experimental outcomes demonstrate that Riesz Transform, RBC, and PCA consistently yield the highest accuracy rates, making them preferable options for future research.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) require substantial memory and bandwidth to retrieve data, making them costly to deploy in resource-constrained environments. A viable solution is compressing DNNs, which can significantly reduce their size while preserving performance. Research in this field has generated interest. We conducted a comprehensive review of DNN compression techniques and provided an in-depth analysis of the most effective methods in this area. Furthermore, we introduced an open-source framework called OMSC for evaluating the accuracy and performance of compression solutions. We utilized OMSC to assess and compare the 8 DNN compression methods listed in our study, which are briefly introduced as follows: model pruning, quantization, filtering, embedding, neural tuning, distillation, compact architectures, and special accelerators. We examined the strengths and weaknesses of these techniques, discussed their applicability and reviewed the latest developments in DNN compression research. Based on our empirical findings, we suggested potential future directions for improving DNN compression efficiency.

Protein structure prediction has made significant progress in recent years, thanks largely to the combination of Rosetta and DeepMind's AlphaFold. While Rosetta's refinement methods play a crucial role in achieving high accuracy, particularly in high-resolution structures, they still pose a limitation for proteins classified as low-quality. To address this limitation, our team developed ProCS, a new refinement method based on Protein Structure Prediction with Collective Sampling, which offers a more efficient search process for exploring protein conformation space. ProCS demonstrates improved robustness and flexibility in its prediction capabilities. When integrated into the Rosetta pipeline, ProCS significantly outperformed existing refinement methods, particularly for challenging structures. Furthermore, our team validated ProCS's utility by applying it to the prediction of protein binding sites, demonstrating improved accuracy and new possibilities for structure-based design. ProCS's source code is available for public access on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/CompProteinGroup/ProCS.

In the realm of Deep Learning, the choice of optimization objective is typically considered crucial, yet lesser discussed are the properties of the loss function itself. This paper investigates how various loss functions impact a model's generalization performance, employing KL Divergence in a text classification task as a under-represented yet effective option. The research reveals that incorporating KL Divergence into the training objective enhances both in-domain and out-of-domain performance, particularly for multi-label data. Furthermore, the study's findings suggest that augmenting the soft labels with latent topics can improve the generalization of models trained with cross-entropy.

We examine the basing parquet model, which is derived from the Hamiltonian, in comparison to the standard parquet model, specifically looking at their amplitudes and properties such as conservation and crossing symmetry. It's demonstrated that the base parquet amplitude fulfills the requirements of crossing symmetry, whereas the standard parquet amplitude fails to meet this condition, instead being expressed as a special case of the base parquet amplitude with additional constraints. Moreover, the base parquet model includes an additional virtual particle channel not present in the standard parquet model. As a result, the base parquet model is capable of generating four-particle amplitudes with positive interpolating properties, in contrast to the standard parquet model, which produces amplitudes with positive parity but fail to serve as four-particle scattering amplitudes.

We investigated the structural, spectroscopic, and electronic properties of one-layer TiSe2 using a highly sensitive vibrational spectroscopy technique called Raman spectroscopy. Our studies showed that this material exhibits a unique charge-density-wave state at low temperatures, which can be triggered by pressure. This charge-density-wave state coexists with an unusual type of electronic and phonon interaction, as evidenced by the creation of new vibrational modes at the low-frequency end of the Raman spectrum. These vibrational modes arise due to the interaction between the electronic holes and phonons, as well as the interaction between phonons of different types. This charge-density-wave state is stabilized by an inherent electronic instability, as indicated by the presence of two distinct regions in the Raman spectrum that are associated with phonon and electron/phonon interactions respectively. Our findings reveal that exciton condensation plays a key role in triggering this phonon and electron/phonon interaction, as well as the creation of the charge-density-wave state, as opposed to an electron-hole instability, as some theories suggest previously.

Emergency dispatchers can obtain essential details from victims' relatives and bystanders through text-based risk reporting systems, but the information they gather may vary depending on the type of incident. To create more effective training data for these dispatchers, we conduct an analysis of the content typically provided by individuals in different scenario scenarios. By examining the language patterns in two large datasets from the US and Australia, we identify the typical features and vocabulary associated with each incident type and also identify some unexpected commonalities in the content collected in various situations. This research can help develop automated systems for detecting risk situations and gather relevant information more quickly and accurately.

Previous assumptions about dimensionless parameters in superconducting materials have been challenged by findings suggesting that the magnetic susceptibility in these materials is not constant. These suspicions stem from study results showing that the change in zero-frequency specific heat in these materials does not always proportionally relate to the Fermi velocity, particularly in cases with non-trivial Fermi surface topologies. In this study, an analytical model of superconducting properties has been developed, enabling a direct calculation of the magnetic susceptibility in terms of Fermi surface geometry. By applying this model to several well-known materials, including $\alpha$-Sn, Pb, and Chevrel phase Ni$_{1.5}$Mo$_{0.5}$Sn$_{1.5}$, our analysis confirms that the magnetic susceptibility indeed varies significantly with temperature, even for materials with a simple Fermi surface geometry. These findings are in alignment with previous numerical studies, paving the way for the development of a superconducting theory in which dimensionless parameters are not necessarily constant.

Active learning algorithms seek to efficiently label a limited subset of data
with the ultimate goal of reducing the cost of supervised training.  Minimax
entropy-based active learning algorithms estimate a posterior distribution by
minimizing the conditional entropy of a set of unlabeled data given a set of
labeled data.  Building upon this concept, we introduce a new semi-supervised
minimax entropy-based active learning algorithm that iteratively adjusts labeled
and unlabeled data to optimize a posterior distribution. Traditional AL algorithms
rely on an approximate inference method to estimate uncertainty and diversity,
but our new algorithm directly optimizes a posterior distribution, bypassing these
approximations.  We compared our new algorithm to state-of-the-art AL algorithms on
four datasets and found that it consistently outperforms traditional AL algorithms,
with an average improvement of 14%.  Notably, we observed that our new algorithm
performs well even with a limited number of iterations.

The unique character of a voice or instrument, known as timbre, plays a crucial role in how we distinguish one person from another, and it's also what makes a song sound distinctive. In this study, we explored how song timbre changes from the 1930s to the 2000s using a large database of audio recordings. By analyzing the musical structure of hundreds of songs across different decades, we identified recurring patterns in the similarity of timbre within and across song genres. Our results showed that these similarity patterns are not random random fluctuations, but rather follow a specific order, shaping the sound of popular music over time.

Consider an infinite stochastic process $\{X_n, S_n\}$ with $\mathbb{Z}$-alphabet, where $S_n$ denotes the empirical probability of $\{X_0, \ldots, X_{n-1}\}$, and let $\{A_s, 0  u < s < u+1\}$ be a collection of random sets in $\mathbb{Z}$, where $u$ is a positive real number. We prove that, under the assumption of $\{X_n, S_n\}$ being irreducible and ergodic, the probability that the cardinality of $A_{S_n}(1, \infty)$ remains bounded as $n \to \infty$ is either 0 or 1. In the case of $\{X_n, S_n\}$ being a dependent sequence, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the probability of the set's cardinality remaining bounded as $n \to \infty$. As applications of our main findings, we examine an ergodic Markov chain with a countable $\mathbb{Z}$-alphabet and prove that, under certain conditions, the probability that the cardinality of the set $\{k: X_k = j\}$ for some $j \in \mathbb{Z}$ remains bounded as $k \to \infty$ is either 0 or 1. This report builds on an existing framework for semantics called proof-theoretic semantics. We have adapted it to incorporate complex relationships between fundamental concepts in mathematics, such as the relationships between axioms and theorems. We view these concepts as contained within a hierarchy, with more advanced concepts stemming from previously established ones. We believe that the natural direction of these relationships reflects their significance, effectively making them hierarchical and ordered. We have developed methods to analyze and represent these relationships in a semantic framework, including tools for translating the relationships between axioms and theorems of a system to an extended version of the system. These extensions allow for the representation of additional metaphysical and semantic properties. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our methods by applying them to reasoning systems and examining the relationships within that context.

Our theory revolves around the premise of leveraging human comparison-based feedback in reward learning. We develop multiple iterative protocols that enable agents to achieve optimal solutions in sampled scenarios. We also demonstrate that utilizing comparative feedback enhances the computational efficiency and convergence rate of reward learning compared to individual evaluative feedback, thereby showcasing its significant practical implications.

The Smyth powerspace is defined as a subcategory of the category of topological spaces with the Smyth monoidal product, consisting of subspaces of compactly-smooth spaces, equipped with the Smyth topology.  We observe that the Smyth powerspace construction does not preserve core-compactness in general.  On the other hand, for core-compact spaces, the Smyth powerspace of a core-compact space is specifically a δ-limited topological space, and its δ-limits can be meaningfully defined, leading to the development of an abstract framework for δ-limited spaces.  We propose that this framework be utilized as the basis for a separate category of spaces, separate from the original Smyth powerspace category.

The behavior of vortex loops within a two-dimensional fluid is investigated in this study. A novel approach to understanding the dynamics of these loops is developed, starting with a detailed analysis of their topological characteristics and the creation of a dedicated configuration space, which is found to have a rich geometric structure despite limitations imposed by point markings. A detailed examination of the loop's translation, rotation, and stretching dynamics within the fluid is presented, along with an in-depth analysis of the formation of enclosed regions. A surprising connection is discovered between the loop's configuration space and the area it encompasses, which is found to consistently scale in a non-universal manner regardless of the loop's shape. A thorough comparison is also made between the dynamics of vortex loops and branched polymers, highlighting both similarities and differences.

A causal AIPW estimator has been widely used to address the unconfoundedness assumption in observational studies, enhancing the efficiency of estimators. Previous research highlighted that AIPW itself isn't unbiased without AIPW-style regularization, suggesting AIPW acts as a type of pre-processing step, refining the initial estimators. Building upon this understanding, our study investigates how various kinds of regularization affect the AIPW estimator's performance, using both synthetic and real-world data. Results show that when the number of predictors is large, the L1 regularization has superior properties compared to L2 regularization. Additionally, our research explores the impact of AIPW and regularization on different types of estimators, such as linear and non-linear.

We propose a novel, algebraically-verifiable symmetry in the tau-rho and tau-
pion systems, utilizing the mass of the tau particle, approximately 1.777 GeV, as
a reference point to facilitate lattice calculations. Utilizing a U(3) x U(3) x U(
1) Chiral Effective Field Theory framework, we investigate the U(3) x U(3) chi-
ral symmetry breaking, as well as the U(1) symmetry governing isospin violation.
Our research focuses on the U(3) x U(3) transition matrix and U(1) matrix, while
also exploring the tau-pion transition matrix and isospin-violation matrix. Our
findings indicate that the U(3) x U(3) transition matrix and U(1) matrix satisfy
the sum rules derived from the tau-rho and tau-pion sum rules. Furthermore, we
determine the degenerate U(3) x U(3) transition matrix and U(1) matrix, while
also decomposing the transition matrices into local and non-local components.
Our non-local U(3) x U(3) transition matrix and U(1) matrix exhibit an exponential
decay behavior, unlike the local U(3) x U(3) transition matrix and U(1) matrix.
Our research also focuses on the U(1) transition matrix relating the tau-pion vector
autocor

We examine how baroclinic waves develop and behave in a rotating, vertically stratified system with an inward-sloping upper boundary and a fixed lower boundary. Mathematical models representing this system are solved numerically, focusing on the ageostrophic and non-adiabatic parts of the flow. Our results show wave patterns that reach the upper boundary and alter its slope, leading to changes in the boundary layer and the formation of distinctive wave marks. These phenomena are investigated in the context of changes in rotation and thermal structure.

This study develops a Bayesian framework for modeling and analyzing extreme values, with a focus on estimating the upper tail of a distribution. The approach employs a discrete prior distribution over a sequence of univariate predictive probabilities for each order statistic, with a tunable parameter'm' determining the sequence length. The posterior distribution is assessed at two stages: firstly, based on a sample of independent observations; secondly, as additional data are introduced. The study investigates asymptotic distribution theory using simulation and real-data examples to illustrate the method's performance.

We investigate a challenging reinforcement learning problem where the environment has been corrupted by a malicious adversary. The corrupting agent has knowledge of epsilon, a measure of how much the environment has been altered, but this information is not available to our algorithm. The goal is to develop algorithms that can adapt to a range of corruption levels epsilon and remain efficient in terms of sample use. We focus on a variant of reinforcement learning known as bandit structure reduction, which involves eliminating redundant state variables, and bandit reinforcement learning, which involves adjusting the reward signal. Our findings show that bandit structure reduction algorithms can be robust to corruption levels up to O(root n)/poly(d) without knowledge of epsilon, but this level of efficiency decreases to O(n^(0.5 epsilon)) when corruption levels epsilon exceed 0.05. In contrast, bandit reinforcement learning algorithms can adapt to a range of corruption levels epsilon from 0.05 to 0.17 with efficient sample use, but this level of sample use increases linearly with 1/((epsilon)^(2)) when epsilon exceeds 0.17. The sample use of our algorithms is closely related to the minimax bound, which suggests that these algorithms are nearly optimal. Our approaches to dealing with corruption involve novel techniques such as the use of spherical caps, geometric modeling, and a new concept in algorithm design known as hyperactive zones. These techniques can be applied to a range of related problems such as robust exploration and causal reinforcement learning.

This study investigates the controllability of the impulsive heat equation, a nonlinear model that arises in various real-world settings. Our analysis focuses on the effects of discrete, sudden changes in temperature within finite-time intervals on the equation's solution. This impulsive behavior is likened to applying specific, brief controls to the original heat equation. We establish a relationship between the magnitude of these impulsive controls and the equation's internal controllability, particularly in the long-term regime. It is shown that as time increases, the required impulse magnitude necessary to control the equation's solution converges to a non-zero constant, thereby indicating that complete controllability may be unachievable due to the nonlinearity of the model.

Recent research has focused on creating accurate out-of-distribution detection methods for image datasets. Although performance improved significantly, discoveries like ImageNet-R, Tau-R, and CelebA-R revealed that existing approaches still struggle with novel and semi-realist data. A new benchmark, called OOD-Bank, is introduced with 12,000 test images spanning 52 categories never seen in training, alongside 12,000 contrast data points from 5 unexpected datasets. Compared to existing benchmarks, OOD-Bank offers more realistic contrast data and a larger pool of novel categories. Notably, even the top-performing methods failed to achieve 95% accuracy on this new benchmark, with some methods performing as poorly as unsupervised methods. By sharing OOD-Bank and providing implementations of evaluated methods, this study aims to foster further research into detecting anomalies in image data.

In systems driven by motor proteins, force production is often influenced by the motor's rotation and power stroke mechanisms. Studies examining force production have primarily focused on the role of power strokes; however, little is known about the effect of rotational movements on this process. To investigate this further, a nanomechanical tunneling probe was used to study force production in an asphaltum-based system that utilizes a rotational drive mechanism. Results showed that rotational movement generates distinct force spectra compared to power stroke mechanics, and these forces can significantly impact the system's dynamics. Ultimately, understanding the relative contributions of these mechanisms will be essential for accurately modeling force production in biological systems.

The field of language-based control focuses on utilizing formal languages and their operators to create control mechanisms, with one-way and two-way transducers being primary tools for this purpose. Previous research demonstrated that any non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be replaced with a bounded, regular one-way transducer that mimics its behavior. In contrast, this study reveals that some non-deterministic two-way word transducers cannot be replicated using a bounded, regular one-way transducer, even with the aid of a resynchronizer. Additionally, this paper explores variations on this challenge, introducing a new concept and demonstrating its complexity by showing that it cannot be simplified.

Our analysis reveals that there exists a more efficient algorithm for computing a single entry of the f-Convolving matrix, requiring less computation compared to calculating the entire convolution. The new algorithm has a better time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n\log^3(n))$ compared to the previous known complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n^2\log(n))$. The improved algorithm utilizes fast Fourier transformation techniques and a novel decomposition technique, and we also introduce a modified Fast Fourier Transformation approach applicable to the given frequency spectrum.

We have conducted atmospheric analysis of the atmosphere of GJ 229B, a Jupiter-mass object located 18.8 pc from Earth, located in a binary star system and surrounded by a misaligned disk. We applied a standard atmospheric model, using data from a single, deep transmission spectrum collected by the JWST, and found that the atmosphere of GJ 229B contains water vapor and lacks methane and carbon monoxide. We calculated the presence of methane to be less than 0.8 times the concentration compared to a Jupiter-like atmosphere, and completely absent carbon monoxide. We observed that the gas surrounding the disk of GJ 229B contains water vapor, but lacks other substances compared to a Jupiter-like atmosphere. We calculated the concentration of methane in this region to be less than 0.7 times the concentration compared to a Jupiter-like atmosphere, and completely absent carbon monoxide. We noted that the object's low-equilibrium temperature monoxide concentration may be present in GJ 229B's atmosphere, but this is not confirmed by the current data. We observed that the object's atmosphere and surrounding disk exhibit different relationships between gas and dust, with the object's atmosphere containing less dust than the surrounding disk, and where water vapor in the object's atmosphere has lower absorption strength compared to a Jupiter-like atmosphere. We noted that the object's temperature structure, when compared to a Jupiter-like atmosphere, could explain the difference in this phenomenon. We noted that the object's atmosphere and

The potential existence of tetraquark states within color-septentriptych models is explored, where a complex potential is derived from 't Hooft's reduced symmetry constraints and instanton sum rules. By examining the spectral density, it becomes clear that the presence of tetraquark states depends on specific characteristics, including the relative magnitudes of diagonal and off-diagonal potentials and their interactions with quark antisymmetrization. In general, finite off-diagonal potentials can prevent the formation of tetraquark states. Moreover, spectral densities suggest that, in this framework, square-root hypercolor is not sufficient to produce bound tetraquarks.

We've made use of the $W$-$Z$ box diagram to calculate $C$P-violating observables in electroweak boson interactions, finding these predictions to be highly precise within the Standard Model. This allows for a more stringent test of the SM or new physics theories with small additional contributions, as even a relatively large phase in the neutrino sector is constrained to be less than $0.10$ rad. Furthermore, future experiments may be able to detect a potential deviation from unity in $C$P-violating phase observations, which would be essential for differentiating between SM and various new physics scenarios, particularly in two-Higgs doublet and left-right models.

We develop a straightforward model, the well-mixed model, to estimate aerosol particle dispersion and settle time around an infected person, based on parameters like breathing rate, walking speed, and a critical air quality standard. This model aligns with more intricate simulations, with a small difference in predicted aerosol concentrations. We use the well-mixed model to calculate effective particle dispersion and escape times in various scenarios, including open outdoor spaces, pedestrian walkways, and public transportation. These calculations suggest a minimum safe distance from an infected person could be approximately 3.5 meters.

The aim of this study is to examine the influence of core excitations within the $\beta$-decay of $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te through the use of the ISOL-DIP mass separator and the active vibration of a Si drift detector. The researchers discovered that transition probabilities in even-even core states are highly sensitive to core excitations and can be predicted through the combined analysis of the nuclear mass and gamma-ray transitions. The study found strong evidence for core excitations in both $\beta$-decay transitions and identified novel excited states within even-even targets, which can be attributed to 2 particle 1 hole states resulting from the coupled $\beta$- and core excitations. The data collected supports the theory that transition strengths in even-even core states are directly proportional to the energy of the initial core state.

This research presents two new theorems that enable the automatic detection of violations in established exchange programs established in 2021. Our approach extends the concept of exchange programs to encompass a broader range of scenarios, including but not limited to, network security and position alignment. By leveraging these uniqueness theorems, we create a viable decision-making strategy for designing and implementing 'honest-misbehavior' strategies, potentially exposing program violations. Our automated detection method is demonstrated through case studies involving the "Bull in China Shop" scenario and a security-related case study.

The masses of rare $F$-wave bottom mesons, specifically bottom mesons with an $s$ quark, were predicted in a study aimed at exploring Regge trajectories using the $q$-state heavy-light meson regime. The regime is characterized by the presence of specific symmetry rules that allow for the calculation of energy levels. Notably, the study focused on mesons consisting of an $s$ quark and a heavy $b$ quark, often found in bottom mesons. The research used the principles of the $U$-spin symmetry in SU(3) symmetry to derive mass relationships for these mesons. From these relationships, the study was able to determine the masses of unknown mesons and compare them to predicted values obtained through other methods, including those from the $Q$-Qbar potential model and lattice simulations. The study's results aligned with theoretical predictions, suggesting consistency between theories.

We refine the connection between the periodic simplicity of a number and the size of its decimal expansions, narrowing the range of possible exponents in Szabados's conjecture based on the pattern's intricacy. If the pattern is uncomplicated, we verify the original estimate but find that a more delicate balance arises with more complex patterns, yielding a larger upper bound for the exponent.

A data-driven dimensionality reduction technique known as Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) has gained significant traction in numerous fields for extracting a system's spatiotemporal dynamics. We introduce the Time-Alternating Least Squares DMD (talsDMD) kernel, which builds upon traditional DMD and works with nonlinear systems represented by the kernel trick. Our method specifically utilizes the kernel trick on the Time-Aalternating Least Squares (tals) algorithm, taking the optimized matrix and projecting it back into the original space via the reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By doing so, talsDMD enhances DMD in several key ways, offering more robustness, enhanced performance, and a reduced risk of singularity. Additionally, talsDMD extends the interpretability of DMD, enabling the identification of nonlinear interactions and time-alternating dynamics. We demonstrate the efficacy of talsDMD across a diverse range of flow problems, including turbulent flows, conditional stochastic flows, and real-world industrial flows.

The evaluation of chess openings and player skill levels has long been a complex challenge. To uncover the underlying patterns of fitment in the game, we applied the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm to analyze moves made in the Stockfish chess database. Our data analysis revealed distinct regions of fitment in the game, corresponding to intuitive phases of play where basic rules govern movements, and where fitnes scores are influenced by the level of novice players. As players progress to more strategic phases, fitnes scores become determined by the skills of experienced players. To validate our findings, we conducted a series of experiments, including a simulation of a chess tournament, to demonstrate that the algorithm can accurately assess player skill levels and suggest new criteria for evaluating chess players.

The Accretion Induced Collapse (AIC) of a compact object, such as a white dwarf or neutron star, plays a crucial role in the development of various astrophysical phenomena, including Binary Hertzsprung Short Period X-ray Variables (BHPSXVs) and Second-Generation Supernovae. Our research aims to explore the impact of gravitational wave-induced fluctuations in binary orbits, resulting from minor object interactions, on the AIC process. Using numerical simulations, we examined compact object mergers in binary systems with a secondary component, simulating these interactions through a gravitational wave-induced fluctuation model. Our results indicate that such binary encounters can cause the primary star to eject the secondary object at a distance from the star, and potentially lead to the merger of the compact object with the secondary object in a distant orbit. These findings imply that binary systems may not always provide the necessary conditions for AIC to occur, and that other astronomical events, such as stellar encounters, are more likely to induce compact object mergers.

The Euler-Lagrange equation is a key fourth-order ODE that underpins numerous physical models, yet determining its first integrals (invariants of the motion) for complex models like the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator has proven elusive. A new research paper develops a novel computational method to find first integrals for any higher-order Euler-Lagrange equation, including those that are semi-symmetric and conformally invariant. This breakthrough allows for a straightforward derivation of the first integrals of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, as well as the degenerate case, revealing a surprising link to the total energy and a combined'moment of inertia' variable. This innovative work will likely have far-reaching implications within the fields of differential equations, integrable systems, and quantum field theory.

Three-dimensional shape retrieval from two-dimensional sketches is a difficult task, made more complex because sketches often resemble abstract representations of real objects. Traditional methods that rely on 2D features and comparisons are insufficient because sketch and shape representations differ greatly. To bridge this gap, various mapping techniques have been developed to translate sketch features into 3D language, but these methods fall short due to simplified representations. Unlike other approaches, we propose using both 2D and 3D features in a unified framework, believing that direct comparisons between the two domains are more effective. Since sketches are essentially abstract versions of 3D objects, this approach makes sense. Our tests on the widely used ModelNet dataset confirm this hypothesis, showing that combining 2D and 3D features outperforms other methods in retrieving 3D shapes from 2D sketches and vice versa.

The exoplanet HD80606b, a highly irradiated, extremely hot world with a remarkably circular orbit, is an exceptional example that can help scientists understand how planets form and evolve. As the planet passes close to its star during its eccentric orbit, its orbit causes its distance from the star to vary greatly, resulting in the variation of its orbital speed, temperature, and size. Researchers used to study this phenomenon by modeling the star and the planet simultaneously, but these models initially predicted the planet would shrink slightly as the star approached. However, observations contradicted this prediction, showing the planet would expand instead. A new model takes into account the interaction between the star's surface and the surrounding interstellar medium, attributing the discrepancy to a change in the star's surface velocity that affects the planet's effective temperature and size. As the star slows down due to the planet's gravitational pull, its surface material accelerates, creating a pressure gradient that compresses the star's outer layers and increases its radius, ultimately leading to the observed effects. This model represents the first instance of a non-electric force affecting the behavior of an exoplanet in this type of system.

Previous studies revealed a type III singularities within the core of collapsing, radially symmetric and non-relativistic fluids. This time, we've investigated small deviations from the initially perfectly homogeneous mass distribution and found that such small perturbures significantly impact the formation and appearance of the singularity. For certain types of mass distributions, the singularity may not occur at all, while in other cases its location and strength are greatly affected. To understand the long-term behavior of the system, we've developed a new method of analysis that enables us to determine the asymptotic conditions without resorting to numerical methods.

We examine the stability of extremal black holes within the canonical ensemble. Considering a two-dimensional slice of the spacetime, we derive the Hamiltonian and an associated Hermitian inner product, which enable us to calculate the number of states below a certain energy. Our findings confirm that in the grand canonical ensemble, the extremal black hole entropy is maximized. We also demonstrate that for the mass of an extremal black hole to decrease, a specific condition must be satisfied. Furthermore, our results agree with the weak gravity conjecture, providing further evidence for its validity.

Autonomous lifelong learning, a concept introduced in RL-interpretable systems, allows agents to explore environments independently, adapting to any scenario. A key aspect of achieving this capability lies in incorporating intrinsic motivation, emulating real-world agents' desires to master challenges, and properly designing extrinsic rewards for efficient training within a limited number of interactions. We investigate the intrinsic motivation and the role of rewards in autonomous lifelong learning, leveraging a self-adaptive framework that balances a mix of intrinsic curiosity, discovery, and utility maximization. By balancing these opposing forces, the agent learns to navigate complex tasks efficiently, and we demonstrate its practical applications in tackling sequences of changing tasks and episodic tasks where rewards occasionally disappear.

In colored Poincaré gravity, combining differential constraints with the Poincaré algebra leads to the development of new gauge theories for massive and massless particles. The approach allows one to describe both massive particles with the 2+2 dimension of motion symmetry and massless particles with the 1+1 dimension of motion symmetry across all spin categories within a unified framework. The color Poincaré gravity is capable of incorporating both massive and massless extensions of the Yang-Mills theory, with the former corresponding to the massive Yang-Mills theory and the latter to the conventional Yang-Mills theory. A new quantum field theory is suggested, in which the color generalization of the Poincaré algebra serves as the basic algebraic structure.

We offer a comprehensive overview of parameterized algorithms for directed acyclic graphs, specifically focusing on algorithms with treewidth $k$ contractions. Although this class is equivalent to those with vertex cover $k+1$, it is notably more prevalent. We provide detailed analyses of numerous problems, comparing their hardness in various settings, such as parameterized, co-parameterized, and extended co-parameterized complexity. Notably, we demonstrate the first parameterized hardness proof for the Clique-Deletion problem on directed acyclic graphs with treewidth $k$ contractions. We also investigate the fractional hypertree width, a recently introduced graph parameter. For $q \ge 2$, we show the Clique-Deletion problem with vertex sets of size $k$ mod $q$ is hard for fractional hypertree width beyond the treewidth threshold. Our work is accompanied by an implementation, which can be found at https://github.com/CsUnicamp/Parametric-Directed-Acyclic-Graphs.

In the multicellular systems biology field, predicting cell migration behaviors is a key challenge. Existing methods often rely on intricate simulations but provide limited insight into the underlying biological processes. A more effective approach called MemoNav is presented, which utilizes a memoization technique combined with deep learning navigation. By leveraging previous partial solutions to accelerate computation, MemoNav significantly boosts performance while maintaining high accuracy. Essentially, MemoNav encodes global information from past simulations into local maps, effectively treating the global map as a collective memory. This innovative strategy enables the system to learn from global information, bypassing the need for extensive, time-consuming optimization. Compared to traditional methods, MemoNav demonstrates superior scalability, efficiency, and robustness in predicting cell migration. Specifically, MemoNav outperforms existing systems by 3.31, 3.83, and 3.92 times in prediction tasks involving migration, shape changes, and combined events.

Future hybrid fifth-generation (5G) cellular networks will incorporate unlicensed millimeter-wave spectrum alongside 5G New Radio (NR). To utilize this spectrum efficiently, next-generation wireless systems must leverage advanced techniques such as beamforming and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). In this context, we develop and analyze a novel hybrid access scheme for integrated 5G-5G New Radio networks, enabling multiple 5G base stations to share a 5G New Radio baseband channel via NOMA. Under the assumption of equal power allocation, we establish a general mathematical framework for analyzing the achievable rates in this setting. Then, we derive the asymptotic rate performance for two distinct scenarios: equal power allocation with maximum ratio combining and equal power allocation with SIC. The results indicate that when the power allocated to the 5G New Radio user exceeds the 5G user, the 5G New Radio user achieves full diversity, whereas the 5G user experiences reduced diversity. The findings support the use of unequal power allocation to maximize 5G New Radio performance.

The study explores a simple model of globally coupled oscillators, where individual units are influenced by a short-range interaction and part of a large group that experiences a diffusive coupling, all set against a background of a long-range interaction effecting a global mean field that can assume various spatial patterns. Our analysis shows that under specific conditions, the system's steady-state patterns shift from uniform to complex, spatially heterogeneous configurations, where local group dynamics play a crucial role in determining the distribution of these states. We identify and investigate two types of heterogeneous patterns: one exhibiting gradient structure and the other with disparate spatial regions. Our findings indicate that the system can simultaneously display both patterns, with the coexistence determined by distinct parameters. To understand these patterns, we rescaled them to a reduced representation, revealing the underlying universality and demonstrating how the diffusive coupling affects the resulting state. Our work sheds light on how local interactions, though short-ranged, can give rise to global, complex patterns through mutual influence and adjustment.

The exponential growth of entanglement entropy in random quantum systems, like the Fisher information, can be simplified by leveraging symmetries. This growth can be rephrased as a symmetry-protected tensor product, which remains invariant under a specific group of operations. Introducing one such tensor, $O_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k},t)$, related to the Fisher information, we show it's possible to reduce the rank of this tensor by a third, along with the dimension of the involved Hilbert space, all while preserving the information that describes its growth. Utilizing this reduced tensor, we're able to derive an expression for the leading term of the Fisher information, $I_F(\rho,t)$, in the large-time limit, for the specific model at hand, without resorting to the input from the SYK model. Furthermore, we've explored the properties of this reduced tensor, and its conjugate, in relation to the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues, as well as its eigenvalues itself.

The final word on the Hoyle state's final word has been spoken. A comprehensive analysis of the Hoyle state's 10.79 MeV excited state within $^{12}\,\mathregular{C}$ has been conducted, incorporating the latest and most accurate theoretical calculations from the No-Core Shell Model interaction, as well as experimental decay data from high-energy particle-gamma coincidence spectroscopy. These studies demonstrate that the Hoyle state primarily exists as a unique cluster state composed of three $^{4}\,\mathregular{He}$ clusters. While non-sequential decay patterns account for a relatively small fraction of experimental branching ratios, they significantly influence the perceived cluster characteristics. A distinctive feature of the non-sequential decay is the simultaneous emission of three protons and one gamma-ray from a relatively low-energy proton source. Our research identifies the 0s 0p orbital within the $^{12}\,\mathregular{C}$ core as the primary non-sequential decay contributor. Given its prominence, this phenomenon is anticipated to be easily detectable using a high-energy proton-recoil spectrometer. Our findings also reveal that the Hoyle state's cluster structure is remarkably resilient against strong two-body interactions. Additionally, we derive new insights into the spin-orbit interaction within the $^{12}\,\mathregular{C}$ nucleus. Our work is also anticipated to stimulate the development of new theoretical frameworks, as well as influence future experimental investigations.

The fracture of brittle materials is thoroughly examined using cohesive zone models that describe the crack tip's behavior as a shrinking crack and the propagation of a moving crack. The models we analyze further account for two essential factors: (i) the presence of intrinsic length scales within the fracture process and (ii) the increase in stress ahead of the crack tip due to high loading levels. Through our analysis, we demonstrate that these two factors have a significant impact on crack propagation and fracture at all scales, and we derive new expressions for fracture energy and fracture toughness based on Griffith's criteria. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive explanation of how extrinsic length scales emerge from the cohesive zone model and demonstrate that these scales depend on material parameters such as fracture process energy and on the stress level ahead of the crack tip. Furthermore, we show that higher loading levels lead to the development of larger extrinsic length scales. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for experimental research to investigate these findings.

This study investigates channel capacity under the constraint of causal state information in communication systems, assuming the use of recursive stochastic protocols that have been previously established. We derive an essential mathematical relationship that enables the determination of channel capacity, along with a method for constructing an optimal communication system. We then apply this framework to two specific scenarios: a discrete-time channel with a finite state space, and a continuous-time channel that follows a Brownian motion. Our analysis shows that the channel capacity can be significantly increased when taking advantage of causal state information, and that the optimal communication system is often highly complex, requiring a sophisticated relationship between the encoder and a causal estimator of the channel state.

In B20-type compounds like MnSi, FeGe, and FeP, the combination of spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity often results in a unique interplay that preserves symmetry. We investigated the superconducting properties of these materials, focusing on a superconducting state that features a specific topological structure. Our analysis shows that as magnetic fluctuations grow in scale, the topological structure of the superconducting state transforms from a smooth, connected pattern to a collection of isolated points. Despite the scale of the interactions, the superconducting state may exhibit a conventional response to an external magnetic field or an unusual behavior based on a microscopic property called the Wiedemann-London charge. Additionally, the unique structure of the superconducting state may give rise to unusual effects, such as distinct jumps in the temperature at which superconductivity sets in or melts, and a unique relationship between the magnetic field at which a specific phase transition occurs and the temperature at which superconductivity sets in or melts.

In the SemTab challenge, we organized a dataset rich in semantic table information to test participants' ability to complete eight diverse tasks. Comprising four sub-tasks, involving data modification with up to five row interchanges, along with three extraction tasks that required identifying specific cell contents. Out of eleven submitting teams, nine successfully completed the data modification task and eight completed the data extraction task. Our evaluation showed that human performance could nearly match that of machines, with the best system performance exceeding that of human performance by a mere 2%. The data from this challenge has been made available at https://semtabx.github.io/, where you can find our full report detailing the competition and its results.

This paper presents a fundamental re-examination of Quantum Mechanics, aiming to address common criticisms of its underlying structure. We argue that the inherent use of complex numbers is irreplaceable, but the inherent need for unit vectors can be relinquished. In our revised approach, we incorporate the mathematical rigor of Hilbert spaces, allowing for a clear formulation of Quantum Mechanics. We demonstrate that the conventional boundary conditions, which yield eigenfunctions, are not universally applicable, but derive specific instances for time-independent Schrödinger equations under distinct physical conditions.

Given a connected, undirected graph G and a real number k greater than 1, the k-distance label or metric label refers to an assignment of labels to the vertices of G such that each label corresponds to a node in G where the geodesic distance between them does not exceed k, and such labels exist for all nodes in G. The minimum number of labels required to meet this criterion is known as the metric dimension of G when the geodesic distance is truncated at k. This concept can be found in a study by the second author, where the upper and lower bounds of this metric dimension were established, particularly for k equal to 2.5 in a study by the first author. In this paper, we establish the exact value of the metric dimension for the same graph, where the geodesic distance is truncated at 2.5. Additionally, this study also explores the relationship between the smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian of G, denoted as σ min, and the metric dimension of G when the geodesic distance is truncated at σ min.

The steady-state flow equation can be simplified by integrating the flow domain into separate zones based on hydraulic conductivity variations, and by making assumptions about pressure distribution across these areas.  One common assumption is the piezometric head behaves linearly within each zone.  This work re-examines how the steady-state flow equation is transformed when the fluid moves horizontally and horizontally variable hydraulic conductivity dominates the flow regime.  A weight function and a transmissivity coefficient are defined to derive a simplified partial-differential equation that governs the piezometric head in each zone.  Unlike previous works, we do not make any assumptions about the head distribution, instead, we demonstrate that the partial-differential equation is accurate regardless of the head's non-linear behavior within each area.  We also show that when horizontal conductivity prevails, the piezometric head will be nearly vertical everywhere.

The study utilized a CSTR-O3-UV reactor system to remove sulfur dioxide from flue gases, similar to those emitted from fossil fuel power plants.  Investigating the chemical absorption of O3 on a molecular scale allowed researchers to develop first-principles kinetic models, which were then combined with a CSTR model to simulate the reactor's behavior.  Key factors influencing SO2 removal were initially examined, including initial O3 concentration, UV light intensity, reactor volume, and catalyst loading.  Subsequently, the study delved into the optimization of SO3 formation, focusing on O3 initial concentration, SO2 concentration, and OH loading.  Finally, a technological feasibility assessment was conducted to explore the potential of O3-UV for large-scale sulfur dioxide removal.  Based on this analysis, O3-UV does not appear to be a viable solution for this application due to its relatively low efficiency for a given reactor volume, primarily because of the energy required to produce and utilize the oxidant.  However, this technology may be more feasible for applications that value low emission rates over a small footprint.

Virtual platform segmentation is a key strategy for evaluating multiple design configurations of an integrated circuit without physically rebuilding each variation.  For neuromorphic arrays, however, accurately dividing the circuit into separate segments while preserving connections between neurons in each segment is particularly challenging due to their complex structure.  Prior approaches have been limited to partitioning arrays based on neighboring neurons within a single layer, failing to account for 3D structures and global connections between modules.  In response, we have developed an innovative algorithm for splitting virtual platforms into multiple segments while minimizing the number of intersegment connections and ensuring that local connections within each segment remain intact.  Based on this algorithm, we constructed several virtual platforms for different in-memory computing neuromorphic arrays and achieved segmentation times of a few minutes, significantly faster than previous methods at around an hour.  In addition, we have integrated our algorithm into a design exploration tool and used it to determine the optimal virtual platform partitioning for a specific application, resulting in a 30% reduction in required memory.

We introduce Indecision Trees, a novel learning method characterized by choices
and uncertainties represented as probability distributions. Unlike traditional
decision trees, Indecision Trees process data in a sequential manner, allowing each
node to select an attribute based on an uncertainty measure, such as predictive
entropy or cross-entropy. This results in trees that optimize performance while handling
missing values and imbalanced data effectively. Furthermore, Indecision Trees accommodate
complex predictions through the use of probability distributions and offer efficient training
and inference processes, making them suitable for large-scale applications.

The practical application of any similarity search technique heavily relies on its ability to determine early termination and exit searching once the desired result is found, which is particularly true for query evaluation methods. This paper enhances existing work by introducing a more efficient version of the RQR-r* index, allows for early abandoning in X-means clustering and surpasses the performance of its predecessors.
