A unified, systematic approach for deriving fusion and braiding statistics of any non-trivial unitary or unitary matrix portability category in conformal field theory has been developed. This approach identifies novel pathways for calculating universal entanglement entropy in holographic field theories, provides analytical solutions for entanglement entropy in both critical and non-critical systems, and offers a universal formula for entanglement entropy in non-critical, two-dimensional systems with a lower boundary of any form. Additionally, deriving entanglement entropy in multi-segmented states becomes possible. Several numerical results for semi-circumferential entanglement entropy have been obtained and confirmed by independent methods. This approach is generalized to derive fusion and braiding statistics of non-trivial categorical symmetries in field theories. Two instances of non-trivial categorical symmetry in TQFTs have been explicitly calculated, and their effect on local operators in the related CFTs has been determined. Furthermore, the non-trivial categorical symmetry in the related CFTs can be found when the associated TQFT has non-trivial 2-d categorical symmetry. Additionally, the non-trivial categorical symmetry in the related CFTs can be found when the associated TQFT has non-trivial 2-d categorical symmetry. Additionally, the non-trivial categorical symmetry in the related CFTs can be found when the associated TQFT has non-trivial 2-d categorical symmetry.

Given a finite field, GF(q), with its characteristic not equal to 1, and a set of m linear equations in n variables without any order, we investigate whether the number of solutions can be expressed in a CPT-definable manner. This involves logical notation and can be broken down into several variables. Our main findings are as follows: (1) When m is equal to or greater than the dimension of GF(q)^n, the number of solutions is always CPT-definable. (2) When m is less than the dimension of GF(q)^n, and equations have unique solutions, the number of solutions is CPT-definable. (3) When m is less than the dimension of GF(q)^n, and equations do not have unique solutions, the number of solutions is not necessarily CPT-definable. However, we can formulate a specific decision problem related to this scenario. Our study builds upon previous research by Bolander, and connects it to another decision problem, and also answers an open question from that research. Furthermore, based on a key result from Borlino, we can prove that there exists a computational model, which can effectively handle CPT-definable relations.

We have investigated the evolution of the electronic structure and optical properties of (Eu_1-xBi_x)2Ir2O7 manganite series with varying Bi doping concentrations, 0.3<=x<=0.6. Using photoemission spectroscopy, we found Eu-driven ferromagnetic correlations gradually disappear as Bi doping increases, while Bi-driven band dispersion develops in the valence band spectrum, specifically containing Bi 6s states at -2eV. Our theoretical calculations using DFT+U confirm this trend, with the Bi-driven bands shifting to higher energy as the Bi doping concentration increases. We also observed Bi-driven partial occupation of the 6s orbital unpaired with other states in the Bi K edge XPS spectrum, verifying our findings with theoretical predictions. We further studied the optical properties of these compounds using sum-rules and CAS, with the real-part of the dielectric function showing an increase in absorption at 4eV caused by Bi driving the band dispersion in the valence band spectrum.

We demonstrate that for any set-valued mapping $F$ from a Banach space $X$ to its dual space $X^*$, the property of being Lipschitz continuous ensures the existence of a Lipschitz continuous selection for $F$. Conversely, we identify circumstances under which a Lipschitz continuous selection for $F$ necessarily exists. Importantly, these conditions are satisfied by mappings that are not only Lipschitz continuous but also locally compact and have closed, additive images in the space of closed, and bounded subspaces of $X^*$.

An n-tuple of integers $(a_1,a_2,...,a_n)$ is defined as nontransitive if for any pair of distinct indices i and j, the sum of the numbers in the ith group differs from the sum in the jth group. In this paper, we prove that an n-tuple can be classified as nontransitive if the following two conditions are met: first, the sum of all its elements equals $n\choose 2$, and second, the sum of its elements that correspond to even indices is less than or equal to the sum of its elements that correspond to odd indices. It is then demonstrated that an n-tuple can be constructed to satisfy any given set of mod m equality constraints, where m is a positive integer greater than 1. These two theorems enable the creation of infinite sets of distinct, nontransitive n-tuples.

To optimize software performance, developers can utilize runtime options, 
which are parameters set during program execution. However, the presence 
of these options often leads to unnecessary computational waste. This study 
aims to eliminate unused options at runtime, and the system is referred to 
as the optimal configuration. We introduce an efficient method to eradicate all 
irrelevant options in a linear algorithm, regardless of the code complexity or 
the number of options. This approach initially transforms the system into a 
specialized format, which enables easy detection and removal of unused 
parameters. We also develop a corresponding tool, providing practical results 
for various applications, including Apache Commons, Google Benchmark, and 
SimpleOpt. The tool is available for public use at our website.

A comprehensive study of dark matter particle and nuclear interactions has been conducted, covering a range of scattered angles from the smallest to the largest, and nuclear targets from the lightest to the heaviest, with a focus on the latest experimental constraints. The study employs the Fourier-Bessel expansion method to calculate cross-sections and features a unique cross-reference validation technique. The work demonstrates how future large-scale experiments may be able to detect dark matter particles through ionization effects, even when they primarily interact with nuclei through long-range forces. Additionally, the study generates extensive, easily accessible tables and plots, making the data publicly available to facilitate further research and cross-reference purposes.

We have developed a strategy for teleported quantum entanglement in cavity-based anti-polariton networks, utilizing complex entangled states formed by spatial modes. By combining two approaches - one using standard entanglement paddles and another utilizing time-bin modulation, we have found that the fidelity of teleportation can be significantly improved. Specifically, using entangled anti-polariton states, we have demonstrated higher fidelity (approximately 92%) compared to conventional methods (approximately 85%). Furthermore, we have analytically proven that the teleportation of entangled states formed by spatial modes is inherently robust against dephasing and mode mixing. Additionally, we have explored entanglement paddles based on time-bin modulation, which can serve as a means to control and enhance entangled state production.

We propose a deep learning approach to automatically identify heartbeats in ECG signals, effectively addressing limitations in existing solutions. Although a deep learning framework may seem like an advanced technique, applying it to real-world ECG data poses significant challenges due to noise levels that can reach 50 millivolts. Most existing research has assumed near-zero noise levels, but we overcome this obstacle by developing a robust approach. We utilize two techniques to improve heartbeat detection - one uses a novel non-quadratic sparsity-regularized learning framework to derive robust features from noisy signals, and another applies a conditional random field model for accurate heartbeat time-series analysis. Our deep learning method has achieved a 0.96 F-score of 97.9% in the standard incart20 database, significantly surpassing other state-of-the-art solutions. Moreover, we have demonstrated its robustness by achieving a 0.96 F-score of 96.4% even in extremely noisy conditions with signal amplitudes of 5 millivolts.

We analyze fluctuations in harmonic and anharmonic potentials driven by active forces, reporting a surprising distinction in their behavior. In the harmonic case, these fluctuations conform to a Lorentzian distribution, as expected. Conversely, the distribution of fluctuations in the anharmonic scenario deviates significantly from this lorentzian pattern, exhibiting instead a power-law behavior characterized by an exponent that varies in direct proportion to the activity parameter. This peculiar power-law distribution is compounded by the presence of rare, extreme events that arise from the instability of active force systems, as identified using a Peano curve model.

Recent advancements in 3D facial modeling have led to highly accurate results, yet achieving similar levels of detail in modeling human bodies remains challenging, particularly for photorealistic expressions. Given the intricate nature of human bodies, accurately capturing shape, skin texture, and appearance from sparse image data is a daunting task. Most existing methods struggle to handle the complexity of the human form, but our work presents a solution in the form of a multi-image correspondence learning framework called HUMBI. HUMBI uses a mixture of deep neural network-based shape and texture prediction modules to learn correspondence for multiple joint points, while its shape module also incorporates a joint alignment module that accounts for primary and secondary pose factors. This allows the model to efficiently handle correspondence learning for complex geometric data and improves efficiency by reducing the number of iterations required for joint alignment. Our experiments demonstrate HUMBI's ability to achieve accurate correspondence results on multiple human body joints, while also showcasing its application in photorealistic 3D modeling of human expressions using a sequence of images.

To overcome multilingual model training obstacles, we suggest a novel, flexible framework. It accommodates diverse scenarios such as monolingual, multilingual, and cross-lingual settings without needing extensive labeled data. Our approach leverages control variables to separate which language the model should be trained in and what language it should predict. Experimental results demonstrate that in the multilingual setting, our method achieves comparable performance on each individual language as if it were trained separately, while requiring significantly less data for English-German and English-French tasks. Additionally, in the cross-lingual scenario, our model performs competitively and sometimes better than multilingual baselines on zero-shot translation tasks.

The video super-resolution field has gained significant attention recently, with BasicVSR being a highly-effective method that leverages multi-frame averaging (MFA) to improve performance. However, relying solely on MFA restricts its application on slow-frame-rate video games, where the additional latency becomes unacceptable. To address this limitation, we propose BasicVSR++, a approach that seamlessly integrates MFA and non-local operators without introducing additional parameters. As a result, BasicVSR++ enhances the state-of-the-art performance on Vid4 and X4V videos, while also being efficient enough to be utilized in real-time video games. To validate our approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments and ablation studies that are presented in this paper.

In our investigation, we consider a multi-task reinforcement learning scenario where agents need to navigate different environments. Unlike previous approaches that focus on individual task optimization, we examine the use of a single dynamics model trained across multiple tasks. This typically leads to a preference for easy tasks, as the model may inadvertently become suboptimal in challenging environments. To address this issue, we propose a multi-task reinforcement learning algorithm that maintains a dynamics model and multiple policy options for each task. Our method rewards not only task completion but also varies the learned policies in relation to the demonstrated model dynamics, thus promoting generalized performance through the exploration of alternative actions. According to our experiment results, our approach outperbses baseline strategies in complex multi-task scenarios composed of a mix of simple and difficult challenges.

In a universal model of natural systems, a non-equilibrium heat engine achieves maximum output power when its critical parameters reach a pre-defined state, specifically when the scaling parameter $\lambda$ equals 1/2. Under these conditions, the system reaches a state of highest output power while maintaining a fixed entropy production rate. This critical $\lambda$ value, 1/2, signifies the transition from a system operating in equilibrium to one operating beyond its thermal equilibrium.

This research focuses on evaluating the robustness of power grids against severe natural disasters, specifically hurricanes, by leveraging historical weather data and utility outage records. A major power utility in the southeastern United States provided access to outage data, while weather data was obtained from the National Hurricane Center and the National Weather Service. By combining these sources, our analysis enables the creation of non-parametric models to predict hurricane-related outages and estimate economic losses, aiding utility companies and grid operators in preparing for future hurricanes.

This exploration builds upon Hadamard's three circles theorem for functions with single dimensionality, extending its scope to the realm of monogenic functions in higher dimensional spaces. By incorporating a non-negative weight function, $w$, on the real hyperbola domain $D_+(B)$, and another weight function, $u$, on the confalcon domain $D_(B)$, we establish a rigorous extremal problem. Our analysis enables us to derive optimal ratios for functions meeting specific harmonic layer potential constraints. We confirm that the obtained ratios constitute the lowest possible values, thus fulfilling the requirements of a maximum/minimum extremal problem. We also establish connections between these results and Hadamard's three circles theorem, along with identifying potential applications in the context of special multiply connected domains. To facilitate our calculations, we introduce a special transformation, allowing us to express two-dimensional monogenic functions as a real part of a $4$-dimensional holomorphic function, thereby expanding the function's "workspace" from $D_+(B)$ to the full $B$ ball.

New classes of piecewise affine maps over the unit cube $[0,1]^d$ are constructed in this study by combining generalized Dyck paths with simultaneous rational expansions. The maps are developed further by establishing their basic mathematical properties. We investigate the inherent spaces encoded by these maps, focusing on their relationship with the Dyck system and rational expansion systems.

Future high-luminosity colliders have the potential to thoroughly investigate theoretical models featuring extended scalar sectors, offering an opportunity to study the mass dependencies of these models. By producing numerous scalar particles, these colliders can facilitate the accurate determination of branching ratio predictions, thereby providing crucial constraints on phantom lepton models, where the lepton doublet undergoes a $B-L$ anomaly as a function of mass. In addition, these models can be probed using dark photons and long-lived particles.

A novel modulated complex exponential (MCE) based auto-regressive network (MCE-Arn) is proposed for resonant signal analysis. The proposed architecture, specifically cascaded MCE-Arn (cMCE-Arn), is examined in terms of its applicability to non-resonant signals. The results demonstrate that a cMCE-Arn structure can effectively model quasi-periodic signals like human speech, indicating its potential for speech synthesis.

Recommendation systems are crucial for various online platforms, helping users navigate complex decision-making scenarios by suggesting popular items. Existing methods focus on either user-side or item-side factors, but overlook the interplay between them. To address this limitation, a new approach is introduced, using Unsupervised Biclustering-based Fusion Clustering (USBFC). It divides data into user-centric and item-centric clusters, simultaneously applying these clusters to create a unified, transposed matrix. This transformed matrix is then clustered again into the original items, ultimately uncovering the underlying structure of the data. In contrast to prior collaborative filtering methods, USBFC successfully identifies the overlap between positive item sets without dependence on hyperparameters. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of USBFC on NCF-based benchmark datasets across multiple metrics. Additionally, a detailed analysis was conducted on the structural characteristics of the datasets before and after application of USBFC.

We introduced X-ray activity indices for better tracing $\beta$ Rydberg states magnetic activity across diverse stars and provided a detailed explanation of their characteristics. X-ray indices are optically accessible and can be used in conjunction with other surface activity markers, such as H$\alpha$ and Ca II H&K. These indices cover a range of $\beta$ Rydberg states from 1s2p to 1s3p with energies of approximately 0.7 keV and 3.8 keV, offering a means to study magnetic activity through X-ray emission across a broad spectrum of stars, including the Sun. By comparing X-ray indices and magnetic activity levels measured using spectroscopic signatures for a group of stars, researchers can further understand magnetic activity's fundamental processes, driving forces, and evolutionary patterns.

To investigate conventional and unconventional contributions to zero-energy peaks in tunneling spectra, we developed a method to separate and analyze distinct current pathways at zero bias, using a non-Majorana model with a single mode at zero energy. The conventional contribution, derived from a normal metal - topological superconductor - normal metal junction with Majorana and non-Majorana impurities, is known, but the conventional contribution with only non-Majorana impurities is less understood. The unconventional contribution, on the other hand, is caused by a mechanism other than a Majorana mode, effectively erasing the zero-energy peak at finite temperatures. Our work shows that both the conventional and unconventional contributions can modify the zero-energy peak, albeit through different mechanisms. The conventional contribution amplifies the peak while the unconventional contribution eliminates it. The unconventional contribution can be distinguished from that of a Majorana mode, characterized by its temperature dependence, and identified as a phenomenon involving a non-Majorana state.

A bicategorical framework for topological Hochschild homology is developed, 
which encompasses several key properties and results generalizing from monoidal 
categories to tricategories, with particular emphasis on the notion of shadows. 
The formalism is self-contained and doesn't rely on pseudo-functors or pseudonatural 
transformations, instead expressing essential concepts like HH(Spectrum) and THH 
through first-order axioms.

Our research introduces a novel technique that transforms a traditional style transfer approach based on neural networks into a quantitative method. We achieve this by converting style transfer into a regression task and utilize PCA to limit the complexity of the solution. Unlike existing techniques, our method does not rely on loss functions or gradient-based optimization. We compared our approach with standard methods such as PCA or VAE and found that our technique outperforms them significantly. Additionally, we developed a method to estimate the contribution of each input feature in the style image, enabling us to perform a partial analysis. We conducted this analysis on the Picasso-Ink dataset, finding that approximately 70% of the style features contribute significantly to the transferred style.

This research introduces a multi-layered attention-driven network architecture, specifically designed to identify key objects in videos, to effectively close the gap between short-term and long-term temporal insights, and to focus on relevant ground features. Unlike conventional two-stage deep learning methods that separate object detection and feature description, our proposed framework combines these processes in a single step. Object recognition is the primary goal, and the method uses a ground context as a reference to guide object analysis and exploit temporal correlations. A novel attention mechanism, called context ground module attention, is designed to map raw frame features into a common reference system, and a multi-scale fusion attention is implemented to combine information across different layers. The proposed framework is applied to high-level object recognition and to a multi-scale fusion attention stream, and it is evaluated on action recognition tasks. Experimental results show that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques.

Our research focuses on simulating the dispersion of snow particles in a turbulent atmosphere, typically encountered during heavy snowfalls. We used the LES code, ESMMS, in conjunction with a Lagrangian tracer to study the movement of particles with varying masses, from 3 micrograms to 300 milligrams. In the simulation area, the airflow is influenced by the presence of falling particles, which can affect their own settling velocity, particularly those with high masses. Those particles that are snowflake-like, however, settle independently of their mass and follow the flow's movement before being captured by turbulent structures, ultimately leading to accumulation at the ground's surface. We used Reynolds number to categorize the particle sizes and calculated the Stokes number, which measures the particle's mass relative to its settling time. Particles in the sub-milligram range have a high Stokes number and settle quickly, while being affected by the flow's turbulence. In contrast, lighter particles are carried off course and follow the flow's movement for a longer time. A high Stokes number indicates that particles are dense enough to follow the flow's acceleration, whereas a low value indicates lighter particles that rise or are carried in a different trajectory. Those particles that are snowflake-like have a low Stokes number and settle independently of their mass and follow the flow's movement before being captured by turbulent structures, ultimately leading to accumulation at the ground's surface. We used a statistical measure called the particle's residence time to evaluate its time spent suspended in the air

Recent advancements in deep learning technology have empowered generative models to accurately replicate complex, high-dimensional sensory data, outperforming previous models in various applications such as image and video creation, discriminative learning tasks, and data augmentation methods. Real-world data often exhibits specific characteristics such as temporal coherence, local smoothness, or correlation among features. However, the popular generative model, the Variational Autoencoder, falls short in effectively capturing these dependencies due to its ability to only learn feature-wise relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce the Concept VAE, an enhanced variation of the VAE that learns to capture the structural relationships within data by utilizing graph neural networks to process features. By incorporating this new model, we can learn conceptually connected variables and group them according to their inherent characteristics, leading to the discovery of meaningful graph structures. To achieve this, we develop an intrinsic graph learning approach, where the learned model is used to determine the strengths of connections between variables by optimizing for relevant graph structures. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through multiple applications, including the classification of images, classification of data, generation of videos, and the augmentation of data.

Current data compression methods, relying on lossy schemes that irreversibly discard information, are inherently flawed. To address this limitation, we present the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), a novel two-headed autoencoder design that enables seamless data compression and high-fidelity reconstruction through preservation of redundant features. By maintaining separate encoders for input 'X' and 'Y', the BCAE detects unique representations for each pair of interdependent data points, and uses these to compress 'X' while using 'Y''s specific features for accurate reconstruction of 'Y', and 'X''s features for 'X' reconstruction. This method demonstrates superior performance in compressing interdependent 2D synthetic data and 3D medical images, surpassing conventional compression methods.

To investigate the thermodynamic properties of galaxy clusters as a complex biological system, we employ the Tsallis statistical method in conjunction with the Bateman distribution. This approach enables us to analyze the phase transitions and critical behavior of galaxy clusters. We have investigated the sum of the inverse temperatures of galaxy clusters, represented by the number of sunspots on the Sun, and found that it exhibits a phase transition similar to a magnetic system. Our results are consistent with theoretical predictions, and we have determined the critical exponents for the Bateman distribution. The study of galaxy clusters has become a vital area of research in astrophysics, and understanding its thermodynamic properties can provide valuable insights into the origin and evolution of the universe.

This paper delves into convex geometric hypergraphs, specifically exploring saturation issues and associated saturation numbers for these structures. Building upon a framework introduced by Fountoulakis and Raghavan at SIMC 2012, we have developed new methods to determine saturation numbers for 'wheel-like geometric hypergraphs,' as well as established exact saturation numbers and infinite saturation numbers for certain representative classes of convex geometric monotone path hypergraphs.

New experimental limits are established for the half-lives of hypothetical scalar and pseudoscalar particles that could be generated in the sun's core. These particles, known as alphas or deuterons, are produced through the weak breaking of symmetry and can escape the sun's core if their masses fall within specific ranges. The smallest possible cross-sections for these processes have been calculated and used to set new limits on the half-lives of potential particles. These limits are more stringent than previous ones, with those related to a hypothetical scalar particle significantly improved.

Researchers discovered Trident, a transforming robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey, which changes shape to climb walls.  Its body consists of flexible sheets that unroll and fold to allow the robot to move up steep surfaces.  This unique change enables the robot to change from a flat sheet to a curved, three-dimensional shape and vice versa.  After conducting tests, researchers found that Trident can climb at speeds of 1-3 cm per second, while the Pacific Lamprey climbs at speeds of 0.02-0.2 cm per second.  This capability allows the robot to climb at angles of 25 degrees, which is more than twice the angle at which the Pacific Lamprey can climb.  This research will likely aid the development of robots that can climb at varying angles.

This study investigates the effects of high-frequency ultrasound on colon cancer cells treated with Doxorubicin and Interleukin-2. The goal is to develop a novel treatment approach that successfully targets cancer cells while protecting surrounding healthy tissues. The feasibility of this therapy was confirmed by in vitro and in vivo experiments, and computational simulations were conducted to assess its efficacy and optimize parameters. The findings demonstrate that ultrasound can enhance the delivery of chemotherapeutic agents into cancer cells, and by adjusting key parameters such as frequency and power, the treatment can be fine-tuned to achieve maximum therapeutic outcomes.

This research investigates the trade-off between information age and throughput in wireless communication systems. Focusing on a single-hop transmission, we developed an optimization problem to minimize the information age subject to throughput constraints. By incorporating non-negative piecewise linear functions into the optimization, we were able to derive a computationally efficient solution. This approach was extended to multi-hop transmission by converting the original problem into a series of single-hop optimization problems. Our results demonstrate that maximizing throughput results in extremely high aged information, even reaching the theoretical age limit as time progresses. We also analyzed the impact of throughput and information age under average-age optimization, revealing a fundamental relationship between these metrics. Furthermore, we examined the age performance under multiple access strategies, such as packet joining and packet selection, and derived a lower bound on the age variance under joint transmission.

We demonstrate helicity conservation for weak solutions in various function spaces of the Navier-Stokes equations under minimal assumptions. Unlike velocity, the curl of the velocity does not need to be in $L^2$ for helicity to be conserved. In contrast to a requirement of $L^\infty$ bound on the velocity by 0 in order to ensure helicity conservation, we only need its $L^2$ norm to be less than or equal to 0. This is an extension of a long-standing open problem initially proposed by Chae and Choi.

This research paper centers around the continued development of the optical scenario, where a real function $f$ on the real line drives the behavior of a solution to the Schrödinger equation in the long wave limit, specifically within the space of compactly supported smooth functions. Initially building upon past asymptotic estimates, our analysis reveals more precise bounds, leading to a simplified expression for $f$. This study also explores potential applications and extensions, such as supposing $f$ has a strong smooth variation near infinity, or examining the direct scattering theory for a Schrödinger operator with a potential that decay at an inverse square rate.

As gravitational-wave detectors undergo upgrades to enhance their sensitivity, events involving compact binary systems will be detectable at greater distances and with lower initial orbital eccentricities, placing higher demands on accurate binary eccentricity calculations. We critically examine the existing approach of using P, a measure of eccentricity, which fails in such low-eccentricity scenarios, and propose an alternative method using Q, a measure of harmonic eccentricity, which provides more accurate predictions even at low eccentricities. We demonstrate that systems initially undergoing small eccentricity changes can experience significant variations in their orbital parameters, and show that these changes are well-represented by using a St\"ckel transform. This transform also helps us identify the conditions under which the P-based and Q-based predictions converge. Importantly, we find that for inspiral distances very close to the merger threshold, the final eccentricities of initially non-circular systems can be quite high, up to 0.2-0.3, which is relevant to the upgraded detectors' sensitivity range, and may result in systems not merging as expected based on P-based predictions.

A combination of two advanced techniques, X-ray free-electron laser oscillation (XFELO) re-amplification and undulator tapering, paired with X-ray energy tuning, could potentially lead to the creation of extremely powerful X-ray pulses, reaching intensities in the $10^{22}$ to $10^{23}$ Watts per square meter range. This would create an ideal setup for investigating intricate atomic interactions and generating novel X-ray holographic images of highly structured objects. To achieve this, a specially designed storage ring, known as the SPRAL, with a unique circular helical undulator, can play a key role by facilitating the re-amplification of XFELO pulses while adjusting their energy. The proposed setup could serve as a cutting-edge user facility, offering a wide range of applications across various fields.

Graph event detection is crucial for identifying significant changes in dynamic networks. Current methods employ either a single network model to predict future events or, through data ensembles, utilize multiple network models to estimate uncertainty. Nevertheless, this approach is limited, as inaccuracies in individual models can lead to false predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce an enhanced deep learning framework, DyGED, which utilizes a Bayesian update process to refine event detection in dynamic networks. By integrating multiple models, analogous to multi-agent consensus in communication systems, DyGED's output is a collective prediction that surpasses the capabilities of each individual model. We further demonstrate that our method complements existing approaches, yielding high performance with a low number of models required. Through extensive testing on diverse datasets, DyGED consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

We have modified the Guderley problem to examine how accurately the Rayleigh--Taylor instability grows in different computational codes. To achieve this, we first created a perfect hydrodynamic model of a collapsing spherical point mass with a prescribed inward velocity profile. Next, we introduced a weak area that is susceptible to the Rayleigh--Taylor instability. To ensure that solutions from various codes converge to the same outcome, we established a criterion based on the maximum amplitude of the perturbation. Our results demonstrate that solutions from most codes can converge to each other within a certain tolerance, which is independent of the perturbation amplitude. However, some codes required additional artificial viscosity to achieve convergence. We compared these findings with theoretical predictions and explored the effects of changing parameters such as initial perturbation amplitude, pressure, and fluid compressibility. Moreover, we used the Guderley problem to investigate the limits of hydrodynamic codes under extreme conditions.

Despite recent advancements in explainable AI, there is a significant discrepancy between research advancements and the actual implementation of explainable AI in most industries, including the one we work in. To bridge this gap, our team conducted a study aimed at understanding the current state of explainable AI adoption within our organization. By collecting and analyzing the results of a survey administered to 26 researchers and engineers, we identified key areas of concern and pinpointed several potential obstacles to adoption that were overlooked in existing research. Our study's findings highlight the importance of incorporating requirements engineering techniques to enhance the usability of XAI methods.

In colorectal adenoma diagnosis and grading, pathological examination plays a crucial role, however, it lacks objectiveness and leads to time consumption after surgery. In this study, we investigate the application of deep neural networks in reducing the subjectivity of such diagnoses. We propose a fully automated system, consisting of two main parts: a lesion detection module that localizes and extracts the target region of interest from endoscopy images, and a classification module that distinguishes and grades lesions based on the extracted region. Ultimately, our study aims to improve endoscopy accuracy and efficiency in identifying and grading colorectal adenomas.

This study investigates a fixed-length source coding problem in which the source is subject to strict power constraints. The research considers both deterministic and randomized encoding approaches. A key finding reveals that optimal normalized leakage, achieved by a specific coding method, also represents the maximum feasible compression rate. This outcome is further validated by an alternative proof and extends previously established results in the literature. Additionally, the study explores the broader applicability of its results to source coding problems under distinct constraint types.

We introduce a new hierarchical approach to high-resolution image synthesis using a deep generative model. Our method, which builds upon the VAE-GAN framework, diverges from standard low-to-high-resolution generation techniques that rely on repeated sampling and transformation. Instead, our hierarchical model MrSARP produces images at various resolutions directly, a capability reminiscent of the Multi-Scale Auto-Associative Residual Network. In contrast to previous high-resolution synthesis methods, our approach is more efficient as it doesn't require transforming low-resolution images into high-resolution outputs, a step that typically involves complicated manipulation and is difficult to optimize. Furthermore, our model excels in two key areas: it produces realistic and visually appealing images, and it achieves state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation tasks.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm's performance can be enhanced through two approaches: refining its probabilistic sampling mechanism and streamlining its costly reconfiguration process. Our study focuses on the latter by leveraging Bayesian optimization to guide the quantum circuit's parameter update in the variational solver. By doing so, we demonstrate the efficient discovery of high-quality solutions without the need for an exhaustive search over the search space. Our results show that Bayesian optimization can successfully identify optimal circuit parameters for solving a specific MaxCut instance on the IBM QX5 device, outperforming standard random search and the standard AOA reconfiguration method.

This article presents a novel approach to determining if and where two general ellipses intersect, using only arithmetic operations and symbolic alpha and beta values that represent the ellipses' geometric properties. Based on this algorithm, we develop a symbolic expression to represent the intersection points of two ellipses, allowing for the solution of this problem even when the ellipses are not generable. We then demonstrate how this algorithm can be utilized in a numerical method to solve the intersection of two elliptical curves in the plane, especially in cases where the curves are not converging, making the problem challenging. We also provide a graphical implementation of this algorithm using Wolfram Mathematica, showcasing its effectiveness.

Actor-critic methods in reinforcement learning typically involve an actor that adjusts a policy probability distribution based on a critic's assessment of how well actions are rewarded, with the critic estimating the expected return associated with each action. A fundamental challenge in these algorithms is calculating the density function of the Gibbs measure created from the current q-function, with algorithms like REINFORCER and Neural Enhanced Sampling approaching this problem in distinct ways. This study investigates the convergence of these algorithms and explores their connections, with a particular focus on REINFORCER's ability to learn a tempered q-function while establishing a direct relationship with Neural Enhanced Sampling's use of a time-varying critical probability.

Using the dynamical mean-field theory combined with the self-consistent higher-order approximation, we found that in the two-dimensional Hubbard model with a weak next-nearest-neighbor interaction, small next-nearest-neighbor interaction can stabilize the stripe phase which is challenging to be studied with first-principle methods. Our results indicate that quantum fluctuations play a crucial role in the stripe phase's stabilization through enhancing its correlation with the next-nearest-neighbor hopping. Furthermore, we observed that in the stripe phase, the correlation is primarily associated with the two-dimensional nature of the system, rather than its periodicity.

Vertebral body localization is a complex procedure that influences the accuracy of various medical diagnostics and treatments. A high success rate for this task is crucial when using computerized tomography (CT) scans to identify and operate on spinal abnormalities. In this study, we introduce a new, advanced method for vertebral body localization in CT images that outperforms existing approaches. Our technique enhances the identification rates of vertebrae and their associated discs when compared to state-of-the-art methods. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted experiments on three public datasets and obtained better results than other competing methods. Our technique achieved an average of 92.7 percent accuracy for vertebral body localization, 88.3 percent for disc identification, and 93.6 percent for disc localization.

A universal framework for Markovian models has been developed using the principles of algebraic and topological mathematics. This method involves reducing any Markovian model to a weighted graph, from which asymptotic averages and correlation integrals can be calculated through algebraic and topological operations. This scheme encompasses statistical models, dynamical systems, information theories, and stochastic processes, offering a unified approach to studying these models. Building upon this framework, a general theory of state transitions has been devised, which provides a common platform for comparing different models.

Let $X$ be a toric complete intersection defined by the polytope $P$ with smooth divisors. We denote the relative $I$-functions of $X$ as $I_{t,P}$. We prove in the paper that for any two relative $I$-functions, $I_{t,P_1}$ and $I_{2,P_2}$, there exists an analytic continuation so that $I_{t,P_1} = I_{t,P_2} \cdot \Delta_{P_1,P_2}(t)$, where $\Delta_{P_1,P_2}(t)$ is a rational function, depending on $t$. If $P_1$ and $P_2$ are equivalent, the function $\Delta_{P_1,P_2}(t)$ equals $1$. We also show that the period integrals of a specific vector bundle on $X$, matching a certain weight, are equal to $\sum_{i=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^i}{i!} I_{t,P}^{k+2j}(t)^{2i} \mathfrak{m}_P(t)^i$. Here, $\mathfrak{m}_P(t)$ is a specific element of a Weyl algebra, and $k$ and $j$ are positive integers. This result generalizes a previous conjecture to include higher dimensional complete intersections.

A new method to enhance surface coupling between piezoelectric materials through
optimization is presented. This method relies on transmitting energy between two
materials efficiently, which is established using a fundamental principle and
analyzed in terms of electromechanical properties. By applying this framework to
a specific scenario, research findings indicate that it is possible to boost energy
transfer even when the materials involved have naturally weak interactions. This
approach shows particular promise for applications where high-k materials are
coupled to common substrate materials, such as silicon or sapphire.

We investigate polariton condensates, which behave like light, under spatial and temporal variations. By utilizing a spatial light modulator to alter excitation laser patterns, we demonstrate the condensate's ability to switch between different emission sites, acting like an optoelectric memory. Introducing time-dependent adjustments to the helium gas flow or the position of the wafer within the excimer laser, enables us to manipulate the emission site and its pattern independently. This research paves the way for the development of complex optical circuits and complex logic operations.

Our research focuses on estimating the lifespan of the planetary system K2-22b,  which consists of two closely spaced giant planets orbiting a variable star every 3.02 days and  5.41 days.  Our analysis indicates that the inner planet, K2-22b (a 2.8 times Earth's mass), experiences extreme mass loss due to its close proximity to the star,  leading us to calculate its potential lifetime as less than 300 million years.  This  5-order-of-magnitude acceleration of mass loss compared to Jupiter-like planets in more  distant systems,  results from the increased energy input from the star,  necessitating  re-evaluation of exoplanet mass loss models.  Our findings also suggest that the  outer planet, K2-22c (with a mass similar to or slightly greater than Earth's),  likely formed through a migratory process,  possibly induced by gravitational  2:1 resonance,  and that further observations are needed to confirm this   hypothesis and to study the characteristics of the outer planet in more detail.

We categorize homogeneous polynomials of degree d, denoted as $f$, based on the topological structure of their milnor fiber, specifically the diffeomorphism type of the resulting fiber, and place them into the deformation class of a leading polynomial, with the order of classification determined by the leading term's diffeomorphism type. This classification leads to an understanding of the underlying topology of the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$, and allows for an analysis of which polynomials are topologically equivalent and which are non-topologically equivalent but can be deformed into each other.

This research evaluates three popular libraries for data manipulation and analysis in C# and Python, examining their performance, usability, and consistency across languages. A comprehensive benchmark test involving 44 benchmarking trials was conducted, leveraging real-world datasets from 8 sources to analyze data from 6 diverse categories. Notably, the C# libraries demonstrated superior performance, averaging 2.38 times faster than the Python equivalents, despite Python's inherent speed advantages being mitigated by the NumPy and Pandas frameworks.

Although Galileo is often credited as a trailblazing physicist, his scientific methods were rooted in 16th-century empiricism, which hindered his ability to develop a unified physical theory. This paper reevaluates Galileo's legacy by considering the broader cultural and historical context of his time. Unlike contemporary accounts that emphasize Galileo's pioneering role in physics, this analysis views him primarily as a astronomer, whose Lectiones astronomicae reflected the prevailing empiricist outlook. This perspective is further solidified by his appointment as official astronomer and mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, a role that carried significant political implications. This paper also explores the ongoing debate on Galileo's supposed 'trial' by the Roman Inquisition, separating fact from fiction in the process. Finally, the paper discusses the enduring influence of Galileo's scientific methods on contemporary physics, particularly his contributions to quantum mechanics and relativistic physics.

Efron's concept of q-energy is an expansion of traditional binding energy in non-Gaussian probability distributions, making it a versatile tool for assessing model fit. We introduce a novel aspect of Efron's work, tying the binding q-energy to a cox process, a type of random measure, for the first time. This connection enables us to define a test of model fit, similar to the time series goodness of fit tests developed by Granger and Newbold, but based on Efron's binding q-energy. Notably, our test maintains the asymptotic independence of the test statistic and the estimated parameters, a crucial characteristic. We also demonstrate that, unlike the original Granger and Newbold test, our proposed test is capable of detecting deviations from the model for changing time series data.

The merging of large magnetic structures is driven primarily by edge local enhancement, a phenomenon that's also closely tied to the interplay between two fundamental physical frameworks: macroscopic MHD theory and kinetic theory on a microscopic level. To gain a deeper understanding of this interaction, researchers have developed an approach using direct simulation and matched asymptotics. Specifically, a direct simulation of edge plasma dynamics is combined with an analytical solution of the reduced kinetic model. The resulting work demonstrates how edge local enhancement gives rise to the enhanced dissipation and resonance broadening necessary for the rapid coalescence of magnetic structures. The technique presented here can be adapted to study a wide range of applications by identifying scenarios in which the macro-to-micro physics interaction plays a crucial role.

This study investigates a novel framework for collaborative learning between human and artificial intelligence. We observe two phenomena - "system intuition" and "collaborative strategy adaptation." As the digital assistant gains experience, it develops cognitive approaches and intuitions through problem-solving experiences and human feedback. Additionally, both human and digital assistant capacities evolve in response to their joint efforts. Our analysis showcases the potential benefits of this new framework, highlighting its capacity to produce more efficient solutions and improve communication by anticipating and fulfilling human expectations.
